16989740:
Brewery steps to export Grist events and import them into Encompass Production Orders via the Grist Analytics PdO Import dashboard, plus recipe and Table Translations setup. Requires v25.11+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.11

Pre-Conditions

System Setting: Ensure System Setting 3353 is updated with the correct EDBL Source ID (recommended label: "Grist").

Recipe Configuration:

  • Naming: Recipe Version names must contain the keywords “Brewhouse” or “Cellar” to facilitate matching.

  • Structure: Each Recipe Version must contain only a single Recipe Stage.

  • Method: Set Turn Config Method to Recipe for brewing stages to support multi-turn data.

  • Table Translations: Ensure 1:1 mappings are established for Locations, Equipment, Products (Ingredients and Output), and Brands.

Steps

How to Export & Import Grist Events:

1. Export Data from Grist

  1. Navigate to Export Data in the Grist left-hand menu.
    ​
    ​

  2. Select the Encompass Export tab.
    ​
    ​

  3. Select the desired date range (e.g., "Today") and click Export Data.
    ​
    ​

  4. Grist will generate a ZIP file (compressed) containing 2 JSON files (Grist_Data_Export.zip) to your local computer.

2. Prepare the Files

  1. Click on the download ZIP file. This will create a folder with the same name as the ZIP file containing the 2 JSON files (Grist_Cellar_Export.json and Grist_SubBatchTransferToCellar_Export.json)
    ​
    ​

  2. Identify the specific file containing the SubBatchTransferToCellar event for Brewhouse activities.
    ​
    ​

  3. Rename the files using the download date and a counter (e.g., Grist_SubBatchTransferToCellar_20250623_1.json) to easily identify it during the upload.

3. Import into Encompass

  1. Navigate to the Grist Analytics PdO Import dashboard using Universal Search.
    ​
    ​

  2. Select the Brewhouse tab.
    ​
    ​

  3. Click Upload Files and select the renamed JSON file from your computer.
    ​
    ​

  4. Click Process to begin the import.
    ​
    ​

  5. Result: Encompass will match the data to an existing Production Order or create a new one, populating quantities and marking the Production Order as Completed.

4. Repeat steps for the Cellar export (note: in beta testing)

Encompass will update existing, unverified Production Orders based on the below matching criteria, otherwise new Production Orders will be created if a suitable Recipe Version is found.

  • ProductionOrder.Batch = Grist Event.BrewhouseBatch or Event.CellarBatch, AND

  • ProductionOrder.RecipeVersion.Brand = Grist Event.Recipe/Plan, AND

  • ProductionOrder.Location = Grist Event.Location, AND

  • ProductionOrder.RecipeVersion.RecipeVersion (name) contains: “Brewhouse” if the Event is a Brewhouse event, or “Cellar” if the Event is a Cellar event

Fields And Definitions

  • EDBL Source ID: A unique identifier used to map Grist data into the Production Cloud.

  • Table Translations: A tool that pairs local Encompass IDs with Grist names, allowing the two systems to communicate even if naming conventions differ.

  • Batch Number: The primary key used to match Grist events to Encompass Production Orders. These must match textually exactly.

  • SubBatchTransferToCellar: The specific Grist event type that triggers the Brewhouse data import.

  • Lot # / Batch Code: Values passed from Grist to select the specific inventory layer in Encompass. If a match is found, that layer is depleted; if not, the system defaults to FIFO.

Best Practices

  • 1:1 Mapping: Ensure every ingredient in Grist maps to exactly one product in Encompass. Avoid "many-to-one" or "one-to-many" mappings as the import cannot resolve them.

  • Explicit Mapping: Map all shared data items even if names are identical. This prevents the integration from breaking if an Encompass record is renamed later.

  • Import Frequency: Export and import data no more than once per day to prevent redundant processing of events.

  • Naming Uniqueness: Ensure equipment names (like "FV01") are unique across all locations in Grist to prevent resolution errors in Encompass.

16989745:
Distributor steps in Encompass for creating a custom system alert by copying an existing alert, its report and import routine and changing the criteria. Requires v25.01+ and Administrator or System Customizer role.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • Required User Role: Must be logged into the system with Administrator or System Customizer privileges. The ability to copy and modify system components (Alerts, Reports, Import Routines) is restricted.
    ​
    ​

  • Target Components: The existing Alert, its associated Report, and its Import Routine must be accessible within the application's configuration modules.
    ​
    ​

  • System Knowledge: A basic understanding of the application's Alert Management, Report Designer, and Import Routine functionality is necessary.

Steps

Steps

The following sequence of steps outlines the recommended process for creating a custom alert and report based on an existing template:
​
​

  1. Locate the Report: Navigate to the Alert on the Alerts table (e.g., the inventory alert), and identify the Report it references by selecting the related Import Routine and then the report.
    ​
    ​

  2. Save the Report as New: Access the identified report through the Report Designer or by selecting Import Routine and then the Report from the alert's configuration screen. Run the report and then use the Save Report As option to create a new, unique copy. This new report will be the basis for your customization (e.g., modifying the query to check for values below a specific threshold instead of the original condition).
    ​
    ​

  3. Copy the Import Routine: Return to the Alert's configuration and select the Import Routine associated with the original alert. Use the Copy Import Routine function to create a new routine that will link the new report to the new alert.
    ​
    ​

  4. Copy the Import Routine Subtables: Within the newly copied Import Routine, navigate to the Subtables section and use the Copy Record function to duplicate the necessary table references, ensuring all required data fields are carried over.
    ​
    ​

  5. Review Field Mapping: Access the new Import Routine via the Table Import Wizard. Review the field mappings to ensure the data columns from your new report are correctly mapped to the fields in the alert's data table. Adjust mappings if new fields were added to the report.
    ​
    ​

  6. Copy the Alert: Return to the Alert Management module. Use the Copy Alert function on the source alert to create a new, unique alert.
    ​
    ​

  7. Update the New Alert: Configure the new Alert to reference the new Report ID and the new Import Routine ID created in the previous steps. Modify the alert Message Body and Subject to include the specific details desired (e.g., listing the bins that meet the custom criteria).
    ​
    ​

  8. Test the Custom Alert: Activate the new alert and run the appropriate system job or trigger to test its functionality and verify that the message content is correct.
    ​
    ​

  9. Contact Support if the Issue Persists: If you are unable to locate the copy options, complete the steps, or if the new alert does not function as expected, contact technical support. Please gather and provide the following information for efficient troubleshooting:

    • Exact error messages or codes encountered.
      ​
      ​

    • Screenshots or video recordings of the configuration screens and the unexpected behavior.
      ​
      ​

    • Log files (specifically application/system logs from the time of the error).
      ​
      ​

    • The exact steps taken that led to the issue (e.g., "Clicked 'Import Routine,' but the 'Copy' option was greyed out").
      ​
      ​

    • The date and time the issue was first observed and any recurrence.
      ​
      ​

    • Any changes made to the user role permissions or system settings immediately before the issue appeared.

Fields And Definitions

  • Alert ID: A unique identifier for a specific automated notification rule within the system.
    ​
    ​

  • Import Routine: A defined set of steps or a script that dictates how data is extracted from a source (like a Report) and populated into a target table, which the Alert then uses.
    ​
    ​

  • Report: A configuration object that defines a data query (usually SQL) to retrieve specific information from the system database. This data is the input for the Alert.
    ​
    ​

  • Table Import Wizard: A configuration tool or interface used to visually map the data fields (columns) between the output of a Report and the input fields of the Import Routine's target table.
    ​
    ​

  • Subtables: Secondary data structures or tables referenced by a primary Import Routine that are required to hold related data for the alert message.
    ​
    ​

  • Bin Inventory: The recorded stock quantity for items within a specific storage location ("bin") in a warehouse or inventory management system.

Best Practices

  • Naming Convention: Always use a consistent and descriptive naming convention (e.g., appending _CUSTOM or a unique identifier to the original name) for all copied components (Alert, Report, Import Routine). This makes them easier to identify, manage, and exclude from future system updates.
    ​
    ​

  • Testing Environment: Perform all customization and initial testing in a Non-Production (UAT or Sandbox) environment before deploying the changes to the live production system.
    ​
    ​

  • Version Control: Document the original version of the system component that was copied and note any significant changes made to the custom versions for future reference.
    ​
    ​

  • Granular Permissions: While the Administrator role is required for creation, review if a more granular Customizer role with only the necessary permissions could be used to reduce accidental modifications to core system components.

16989749:
Distributor steps for reconciling the AP Aging Report to the Trial Balance/Balance Sheet: align dates, find when the variance began, and re-confirm Purchases paid by Check Run but not balanced. Requires v25.10+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.10

Pre-Conditions

  • Financial Periods Closed: Both the AP Close and Financials Close processes should be completed for the period being compared (e.g., if comparing as of 9/30, both AP and Financials should be closed through 9/30). This is not always necessary depending on set filters for status.
    ​
    ​

  • Report Date Alignment: The Statement Date used for the Accounts Payable Aging Report must precisely match the date or period-end used for the General Ledger Trial Balance.
    ​

  • Correct Account Comparison: You must be comparing the Total of the Accounts Payable Aging Report to the balance of the designated Accounts Payable General Ledger Account (e.g., 1-00-2200-00 or similar).

Steps

1. Verify Period Closures:

  • Confirm that both the AP Close and Financials Close processes have been run and completed for the period ending on the comparison date (e.g., month-end).
    ​
    ​

  • Failure to close both can prevent certain transactions from generating or verifying the necessary General Ledger journal entries.
    ​
    ​

2. Ensure Date Consistency:

  • Run the Accounts Payable Aging Report and the Trial Balance using the exact same period-end date.
    ​
    ​

  • Even a slight difference can cause a variance due to how different reports pull data.
    ​
    ​

3. Find the Date the Discrepancy Began:

  • Run both reports for consecutive prior periods (e.g., month-end) until they balance.
    ​
    ​

  • The first date they don't balance is the date the variance started. This narrows down the transaction search.
    ​
    ​

4. Examine Transactions on the Discrepancy Date:

  • On the date the variance began (from Step 3), examine all Purchase and Journal Entry transactions.
    ​
    ​

  • Look specifically for:

    • Purchases that have been paid via a Check Run but are in a status (like Received or Ordered) that has not yet generated a Balanced Status journal entry.
      ​
      ​

    • Check Run journal entries that have posted to the General Ledger (verified) debiting AP, but the corresponding Purchase journal entry to credit AP has not posted.
      ​
      ​

    • In the provided example, the variance was a Purchase that was paid and verified via a Check Run (debiting GL) but was still in Received status, meaning the corresponding credit to the AP GL account had not yet posted.
      ​
      ​

5. Re-confirm the Affected Purchase Transaction:

  • If a Purchase transaction is identified as the source of the variance (e.g., it was paid but not yet confirmed/balanced):

    • Reopen the AP period (if applicable and necessary).
      ​
      ​

    • Re-confirm the identified Purchase transaction(s) to ensure the balanced General Ledger entry is created and posted.
      ​
      ​

    • Re-close the AP period.
      ​
      ​

    • Re-run and compare the Trial Balance and Accounts Payable Aging Report.
      ​
      ​

6. Contact Support:

  • If the variance persists after completing the above steps, you must contact support for advanced investigation. To ensure efficient troubleshooting, please provide the following information:

    • Exact variance amount and the date it occurred.
      ​
      ​

    • Exact error messages or codes encountered during closing or reporting (if any).
      ​
      ​

    • Screenshots or video recordings of the report criteria and the final totals.
      ​
      ​

    • The exact steps taken (including the specific Purchase and Check Run IDs) that led to the issue.
      ​
      ​

    • The date and time the issue was first observed and any recurrence.
      ​
      ​

    • Any changes made to the system (e.g., new integrations, process changes, or setting updates) before the issue appeared.

Fields And Definitions

  • Accounts Payable (AP) Aging Report A detailed report (the subsidiary ledger) listing all outstanding vendor invoices, organized by how long they are past due (aging buckets). The total should equal the General Ledger AP liability account balance.
    ​
    ​

  • Trial Balance (TB) A report listing all the General Ledger accounts and their debit/credit balances at a specific point in time. It's used to verify that the sum of all debits equals the sum of all credits.
    ​
    ​

  • General Ledger (GL) The main record-keeping system for a company's financial transactions, with all accounts (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenue, Expenses).
    ​
    ​

  • Subsidiary Ledger A detailed record supporting the summary balance in a General Ledger control account (e.g., the AP Aging Report is the subsidiary ledger for the Accounts Payable GL account).
    ​
    ​

  • AP Close The process that locks the Accounts Payable period, ensuring all related transactions are final for reporting.
    ​
    ​

  • Financials Close The process that locks the main General Ledger and financial statements for a given period.
    ​
    ​

  • Received Status (Purchase) A status on a Purchase transaction indicating the goods or services have been received, but the transaction may not have generated a full, Balanced Status journal entry yet.
    ​
    ​

  • Check Run A batch process used to select and pay multiple vendor invoices, which generates a corresponding journal entry to debit the AP liability account and credit the Cash account.
    ​
    ​

  • Balanced Status The status of a financial transaction (like a Purchase) that signifies a complete and balanced General Ledger journal entry has been created and is ready to post (credit to AP, debit to Inventory/Expense).

Best Practices

  • Routine Reconciliation: Make reconciling the AP Aging to the GL Trial Balance a routine, monthly process after the financial period is formally closed. This prevents small variances from accumulating and becoming difficult to trace.
    ​
    ​

  • Maintain Transaction Status Discipline: Always ensure that Purchase transactions are brought to a Confirmed status promptly, especially when they are tied to a payment. This ensures the subsidiary ledger and the general ledger are updated concurrently.
    ​
    ​

  • Review Payment Processes: If the variance is a recurring issue, review your Check Run or payment processes to confirm that payments are only being applied to Purchases that are ready to generate a balanced GL entry. Paying bills via a Check Run using a minimum status like Ordered or Received can frequently lead to this type of imbalance.
    ​
    ​

  • Utilize AP Close: It is suggested to run the AP Close process then the Financials Close for maximum integrity, as it finalizes the Accounts Payable sub-ledger.
16989750:
Distributor steps to build Encompass Cloud Functions (C# on AWS Lambda) with AI using Local Edit and VS Code with GitHub Copilot: compile, Push To Lambda, test. Needs API Edit permission and v26.03+.

Minimum Version Required: 26.03

Pre-Conditions

Before You Begin

Welcome! You're about to learn how to build custom back-end features for Encompass using AI — no prior coding experience required. Here's what you need to have ready before starting.

What You Need

  1. An Encompass account with permission to edit Cloud Functions - API Edit permission, and a Solution Authentication for that Application/Solution (ask your admin if unsure)

  2. A GitHub account (free) — needed for GitHub Copilot, the AI assistant that will write code for you

  3. A GitHub Copilot subscription — there is a free tier available at github.com/features/copilot — Note that the free tier will have lower usage limits and limit to less intelligent AI models

What You Should Know

You do not need to know how to code. The whole point of "vibe coding" is that you describe what you want in plain English, and the AI writes the code for you. However, it helps to understand these basics:

  • Cloud Functions are custom C# code blocks that run on the server. They let you extend Encompass with custom logic — like sending emails, processing data, or connecting to external services.

  • The browser editor inside Encompass is where your code lives. It handles compiling (checking for errors) and deploying (making it live).

  • Local Edit is the feature that downloads your code to your computer so an AI coding tool can work on it. Changes sync back to the browser automatically.

  • You will not compile code on your computer. The browser editor does that for you.

What is "Vibe Coding"?

Vibe coding means describing what you want to build in plain language and letting an AI assistant generate the code. You guide the direction, review the results, and iterate. Think of it like having a conversation with a developer who works instantly.

Alternative AI Editors

This guide focuses on VS Code + GitHub Copilot, but the Local Edit feature works with any editor. Popular alternatives include:

  • Cursor — an AI-native editor built on VS Code (cursor.com)

  • Windsurf — another AI-powered editor (windsurf.com)

If you choose one of these, skip the VS Code installation steps and follow that editor's own setup guide. The Encompass workflow remains the same.

Steps

Step-by-Step Setup & Workflow

Part 1: Install Your Tools

Step 1 — Install VS Code

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com and download the installer for your operating system.

  2. Run the installer and follow the prompts. The defaults are fine.

  3. Open VS Code once it's installed.

Using Cursor or Windsurf instead? Download from their respective websites and open the app. Both have built-in AI features, so you can skip the Copilot extension step below — but still install the C# extension.

Step 2 — Install the C# Extension

This gives you syntax highlighting and basic language support for C# files. You won't compile locally, but this makes the code much easier to read and work with.

  1. In VS Code, click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (it looks like four squares).

  2. Search for "C#" in the search bar.

  3. Find the extension called "C# Dev Kit" by Microsoft and click Install.

  4. This will also install the base "C#" extension automatically.

In Cursor/Windsurf: the same extension is available in their extension marketplaces. Search for "C# Dev Kit" and install it.

Step 3 — Install GitHub Copilot

  1. In the VS Code Extensions sidebar, search for "GitHub Copilot".

  2. Install the extension called "GitHub Copilot" by GitHub.

  3. You will also want to install "GitHub Copilot Chat" — this gives you the chat panel where you can have conversations with the AI.

  4. After installing, click Sign in to GitHub when prompted, and sign in with your GitHub account.

  5. If you haven't set up Copilot on your GitHub account yet, you'll be prompted to activate it (a free tier is available).

Cursor and Windsurf have their own built-in AI, so you don't need Copilot with those editors. They will prompt you to sign in to their respective services.

Part 2: Open a Cloud Function for Local Editing

Step 4 — Navigate to Cloud Functions

  1. In Encompass, navigate to the Cloud Function you want to work on (or create a new one). This is found on the API Commands table, clicking the 'Edit Code' icon on the left side.

  2. The Cloud Function editor will open in your browser with the C# code editor.

Step 5 — Enable Local Edit

  1. In the Cloud Function editor, look for the Local Edit option.

  2. Click it to download the code files to a local folder on your computer.

  3. Note the folder location — you'll need to open it in VS Code.

  4. Keep the browser tab open! The browser needs to stay open to sync your changes back and to compile/deploy your code.

Step 6 — Open the Folder in VS Code

  1. In VS Code, go to File → Open Folder.

  2. Navigate to the folder where your Cloud Function files were downloaded.

  3. Click Open. You'll see your C# file(s) in the file explorer on the left.

Part 3: Vibe Code Your Cloud Function

Step 7 — Open Copilot Chat

  1. Open the Copilot Chat panel — click the chat icon in the left sidebar, or press Ctrl+Shift+I (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+I (Mac).

  2. In the newer version, you may also use the Agent Mode to have Copilot edit files directly. Select "Agent" from the mode dropdown at the top of the chat panel.

In Cursor: Press Ctrl+L (or Cmd+L on Mac) to open the AI chat. In Windsurf: Look for the Cascade panel on the right side.

Step 8 — Describe What You Want

This is the fun part. Tell the AI what you want your Cloud Function to do, in plain English. Here are some example prompts to get you started:

"I want this function to take an email address as a parameter, look up the customer in our system using the Encompass SDK, and return their account balance as a JSON string."

"Make this function send a notification email when called. Use the parameters to get the recipient email and the message body."

"Add a new parameter called OrderID to the Parameters class, then use the Encompass SDK to look up that order and return its status."

The AI will generate C# code and insert it into your file. You can keep chatting to refine it — ask it to fix things, add features, or explain what it wrote.

Step 9 — Understand the Code Structure

Every Cloud Function has a specific structure that must not be changed. The AI should respect this, but it's good to know:

namespace YourFunctionName — must match your API Command name{ public class Function — the class name can't change { public string FunctionHandler(Parameters myParameters, ILambdaContext context) — this is the entry point; the name and parameters can't change { // YOUR CODE GOES HERE // Use myParameters.EncompassID, myParameters.Email, etc. return "result string"; } } public class Parameters — add custom parameters here { public string EncompassID { get; set; } public string EncompassSessionID { get; set; } public string EncompassDBServer { get; set; } public string Email { get; set; } // Add your own parameters below: // public string OrderID { get; set; } }}

Key rule: Don't change the namespace name, the class name "Function", or the FunctionHandler method signature. You can add custom parameters to the Parameters class and add helper methods below the entry function.

Step 10 — Save and Let It Sync

  1. Save your file in VS Code (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S).

  2. The Local Edit feature will automatically sync your changes back to the browser editor.

Part 4: Compile, Test & Deploy

Step 11 — Compile in the Browser

  1. Go back to the Encompass browser tab (keep it open the whole time).

  2. Click the Compile button in the toolbar.

  3. The console at the bottom will show either a success message or error details.

  4. If there are errors, go back to VS Code and ask the AI to fix them. Paste the error message into chat:

    "I got this compile error: [paste error here]. Please fix it."

  5. Save, sync, compile again. Repeat until it succeeds.

Step 12 — Push to Lambda

  1. Once compilation succeeds, click Push To Lambda in the toolbar.

  2. This deploys your function to AWS Lambda and makes it available as an API endpoint.

  3. The first push may take a moment. You'll see a success message when it's done.

Step 13 — Run a Test

  1. After pushing, the Run Test button becomes active.

  2. Click Run Test. A dialog will appear with a JSON input field:

{ "key1": "value1", "key2": "value2"}

  1. Replace the sample values with real test data that matches your Parameters (e.g., an actual email address or order ID). If it helps, you can also ask the AI back in the editor to help you figure out how to format this.

  2. Click Run and check the console output to see if your function works as expected.

Step 14 — Iterate and Improve

This is the vibe coding loop:

  1. Describe what you want → AI writes code

  2. Save → changes sync to browser

  3. Compile → fix errors with AI help

  4. Push & Test → verify it works

  5. Repeat — refine, add features, keep going

Each cycle gets faster once you get the hang of it. Don't be afraid to experiment — the Compile step catches mistakes before anything goes live.

Part 5: Using the Encompass SDK

The Cloud Function editor has an Encompass SDK tab that documents all the helper classes and methods available to you inside Cloud Functions. These are pre-built tools for things like:

  • Making HTTP requests (BC_HttpRequest)

  • Working with data (BC_Fmt)

  • Encrypting/decrypting values (BC_Fmt.AES_Encrypt, BC_Fmt.AES_Decrypt)

  • And more — check the SDK tab for the full list

When chatting with the AI, mention that you want to use the Encompass SDK. You can even paste snippets from the SDK tab into the chat so the AI knows what's available. For example:

"Use the BC_HttpRequest class from the Encompass SDK to make a GET request to this URL and return the response."

Part 6: Using Environment Variables

Environment variables let you store secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens) and configuration values safely outside your code. They are stored securely on the Lambda function itself and are never exposed in the code editor or version history.

1. Open the Environment Variables Dialog

In the Cloud Function editor toolbar, click the Environment variables button.

A dialog will open showing any existing variables. Existing values are masked as *** for security.

2. Add, Edit, or Remove Variables

To add a variable: select Add variable at the bottom of the dialog. Enter a unique key name and a value.

To edit a variable: Type a new value in the Value field. If you leave the value as ***, the existing value is kept unchanged.

To remove a variable: select the delete icon next to the row you want to remove.

When finished, select Save changes. Each key must be unique — duplicate keys are not allowed.

3. Access Environment Variables in Your Code

In your C# Cloud Function, read environment variables using the standard .NET method:

string myApiKey = System.Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("MY_API_KEY");

Or as a static value at the top of the file:

private static readonly string myApiKey = System.Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("MY_API_KEY");

This keeps secrets out of your source code entirely. You can tell the AI assistant:

"Store the API key in an environment variable called MY_API_KEY, and read it using System.Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable in the function."

Part 7: Saving Your Work

  • Save — saves your code to the Encompass system (does not deploy)

  • Save With Message — saves with a description of what you changed (like a commit message)

  • Compile — checks for errors without deploying

  • Push To Lambda — saves, compiles, and deploys your function live

Get into the habit of using Save With Message periodically so you have a history of what changed and why.

Fields And Definitions

Key Terms & Definitions

Term

Definition

Cloud Function

A custom C# code block that runs on AWS Lambda. It extends Encompass with custom server-side logic and connects to an API endpoint automatically.

Local Edit

A feature that downloads your Cloud Function code to a local folder on your computer, allowing you to edit it with VS Code or another editor. Changes sync back to the browser automatically.

Vibe Coding

A style of development where you describe what you want in natural language and an AI assistant writes the code for you. You guide, review, and iterate.

VS Code

Visual Studio Code — a free code editor from Microsoft. Used as the local editor for working with Cloud Function files.

GitHub Copilot

An AI coding assistant from GitHub that integrates into VS Code. It can generate, edit, and explain code based on natural language descriptions. Offers a free tier.

Agent Mode

A Copilot Chat mode that lets the AI read, edit, and create files directly — rather than just suggesting code snippets. Select it from the mode dropdown in the chat panel.

C# Dev Kit

A VS Code extension that provides syntax highlighting, IntelliSense, and basic language support for C# files. You don't need the full .NET SDK — this is just for editing comfort.

FunctionHandler

The entry point method of your Cloud Function. This is the method that runs when your API endpoint is called. Its name and parameters cannot be changed.

Parameters Class

A C# class that defines the input data your function receives. It always includes EncompassID, EncompassSessionID, EncompassDBServer, and Email. You can add your own custom parameters.

Compile

The process of checking your code for errors. Done in the browser — not locally. Click the Compile button to check before deploying.

Push To Lambda

Deploys your compiled code to AWS Lambda, making it live and accessible as an API endpoint in Encompass.

Run Test

Sends a test request to your deployed function with sample JSON data so you can verify it works correctly before connecting it to other parts of the system.

Encompass SDK

A library of pre-built helper classes available inside Cloud Functions (e.g., BC_HttpRequest, BC_Fmt). Documented in the SDK tab of the Cloud Function editor.

Environment Variables

Secure key-value pairs stored on the Lambda function. Used to keep secrets like API keys and passwords out of your code. Managed through the Environment variables button in the Cloud Function editor toolbar, and accessed in C# code with System.Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable().

Cursor / Windsurf

Alternative AI-powered code editors. They work with Local Edit just like VS Code but have their own built-in AI assistants instead of GitHub Copilot.

namespace

The top-level container for your code. It must match your API Command name exactly. Do not change it.

Best Practices

Best Practices

Talking to the AI

  • Be specific. Instead of "make it work better," say "add error handling so if the API call fails, return an error message with the status code."

  • Provide context. Tell the AI about the Encompass SDK. Paste SDK docs or class names into the chat so it knows what tools are available.

  • Iterate in small steps. Ask for one feature at a time. Get it compiling, then add the next thing. This makes errors much easier to fix.

  • Paste errors directly. When compile fails, copy the exact error message and paste it into the AI chat. It's very good at fixing compile errors when it can see the exact message.

Things to Never Change

  • The namespace name — it must match your API Command.

  • The class name "Function" — the system looks for this exact name.

  • The FunctionHandler method name and its parameters (Parameters myParameters, ILambdaContext context).

  • The LambdaSerializer assembly attribute at the top of the file.

  • If you accidentally change these, the AI can help fix them — tell it "restore the required structure for an Encompass Cloud Function."

Development Workflow Tips

  • Keep the browser tab open. Local Edit syncs through the browser — if you close it, the sync stops.

  • Compile often. Don't write 100 lines and then compile. Build in small increments so errors are easy to pinpoint.

  • Use Save With Message. Leave yourself notes about what changed. Future you (or a teammate) will thank you.

  • Test with realistic data. When using Run Test, provide parameter values that match real scenarios rather than generic "value1" placeholders.

  • Check the SDK tab. Before asking the AI to write custom code for something, check if the Encompass SDK already has a built-in method for it.

Security Notes

  • Never hardcode passwords, API keys, or secrets in your code. Use environment variables to store them securely (see Part 6).

  • To manage environment variables, select the Environment variables button in the toolbar. Values are encrypted and never visible in the code editor or version history.

  • Use the Encompass SDK's encryption methods (like BC_Fmt.AES_Encrypt) when handling sensitive data in transit or at rest.

  • The Parameters class automatically receives the authenticated user's EncompassID and session info — use those instead of passing credentials manually.

Getting Unstuck

  • If the AI generates code that won't compile, don't start over. Paste the error into chat and ask it to fix that specific issue.

  • If you're not sure what's possible, ask the AI: "What can I build with an Encompass Cloud Function that takes an email and order ID as parameters?"

  • Remember: compilation and deployment happen in the browser. If something isn't working locally, that's okay — the browser is the source of truth.
16989751:
Fixing PayLink deposits or credits that don't match the bank after an invoice was edited, deleted, or manually paid while a payment was in flight: unapply and reverse duplicate remittance invoices and reapply.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • Accounts Receivable, Office Manager, or Sales Support with permissions to edit or delete invoices.

  • Deposits or payments are not correct or reflecting what actually hit your bank

  • A customer has an unexpected credit balance on their account because of a duplicate payment

Steps

  1. Identify the Disruption: Review the invoice history to determine if any of the following "High-Risk" actions occurred after the payment was requested:

    • Deleting the Invoice: Removing the record the system is expecting to pay.
      ​
      ​

    • Editing the Amount: Changing the balance after the payment gateway has already authorized a different total.
      ​
      ​

    • Manual Application: Manually applying a check or credit to the invoice while the electronic payment is "In-Flight."
      ​
      ​

  2. Check if there are Duplicate Remittances: Look for system-generated invoices (Remittance Invoices) created automatically to house the payments. These often create False Credits which are duplicated in the system.
    ​
    ​

  3. Check if the paylink term is set to auto-apply payments: Please ensure all paylink terms are set to auto-application = manual or same invoice and amount to ensure payment application does not happen automatically after requesting payment.
    ​
    ​

  4. Perform Corrective Reversals:

    • If a duplicate was created, Unapply the payment from that duplicate.
      ​
      ​

    • Reverse the duplicate invoice to clear the false credit.
      ​
      ​

  5. Re-apply to Correct Targets: Manually apply the unapplied funds to the correct, active invoice IDs to balance the customer’s statement.
    ​
    ​

  6. Verify the Deposit: Ensure the final ECP Deposit matches the net amount settled in the bank.
    ​
    ​

  7. Contact Support: If the system logic has created a loop of duplicate invoices that you cannot break, contact Support with the following:

    • The Original Invoice ID that was deleted or edited.
      ​
      ​

    • The Duplicate Invoice ID created by the system.
      ​
      ​

    • A screenshot of the Field Audit showing the user who deleted/edited the record and the timestamp.
      ​
      ​

    • The specific Deposit Number that is out of balance.
      ​
      ​

    • The amount of money that hit your bank

Fields And Definitions

  • In-Flight Payment: A transaction that has been authorized by the customer's bank but has not yet completed the sync process back into the Encompass ERP.

  • Field Audit: A background log in Encompass that tracks every change made to a record, including who made the change and at what time.

  • Target Invoice: The specific Invoice ID that a PayLink transaction is programmed to pay.

  • Manual Intervention: Any human action (editing, deleting, or manual posting) that overrides the automated PayLink sync logic.

Best Practices

  • "Hands Off" During Processing: Once a customer has been sent a PayLink request, do not touch the invoice in Encompass until the payment is marked as "Succeeded" or "Failed."

  • Voiding vs. Deleting: If an order must be changed, it is better to allow the payment to fail or settle and then issue a formal credit memo rather than deleting the underlying invoice record.

  • Monitor the Sync: If an invoice must be edited, ensure the customer has not yet clicked "Pay" in their DSDLink portal and/or there is not already a payment applied on the original invoice.

  • Training: Ensure all staff members understand that deleting an invoice does not "cancel" a Stripe transaction; it only breaks the link between the money and the accounting record.
16989752:
Distributor guide to when orderIQ forecasts run each week in Encompass, what data syncs first, when suggested orders appear for upcoming stops and how they split across multiple stops. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • OrderIQ is installed and scheduled
    ​
    ​

  • Understanding of customer delivery schedules

Steps

How Forecast Timing Works:

1. Weekly Forecast Cycle:

  • Forecasts are generated weekly, typically early in the week (Saturday night)
    ​
    ​

  • The forecast week runs Monday to Sunday
    ​
    ​

  • Predictions are based on the customer's next scheduled stop date

2. Data Synchronization:

  • Historical data is synced before forecasts run
    ​
    ​

  • This includes: stops, calendars, customer/product combinations, prices, sales, weather, and POS data
    ​
    ​

  • The sync process uses data from the previous week unless running a full import

3. When Suggestions Appear:

  • Suggestions appear for the upcoming week's scheduled stops
    ​
    ​

  • If a customer has a stop scheduled for Wednesday, the suggestion will be available starting Monday of that week
    ​
    ​

  • Suggestions update as forecasts complete processing

4. Stop Date Splitting:

  • If a customer has multiple stops in a week, the forecast is split across those stops
    ​
    ​

  • The SplitSequence indicates which stop (1st, 2nd, 3rd)
    ​
    ​

  • The split follows the OrderSize configuration

Fields And Definitions

  • Forecast Date: The Monday of the week being forecast
    ​
    ​

  • Sync Start Time: Start time for data synchronization (typically ForecastDate - 7 days)
    ​
    ​

  • Next Scheduled Date: Customer's next scheduled stop date
    ​
    ​

    ​
    ​

Best Practices

  • Ensure routes and stops are configured correctly before the forecast runs
    ​
    ​

    ​
    ​

    ​

    ​

16989753:
Distributor steps to vibe code Encompass dashboard Code Blocks with AI using Local Edit in Chrome or Edge with VS Code Copilot, Cursor or Claude Code: preview, tests, screenshots. Requires v26.03+.

Minimum Version Required: 26.03

Pre-Conditions

What You'll Need Before You Start

Vibe coding lets you describe what you want in plain English and an AI agent builds it for you. No programming experience needed — just clear ideas about what you want to create.

Before you begin, make sure you have:

1. A Code Editor with an AI Agent

We recommend Visual Studio Code (VSCode) with GitHub Copilot — it's the most popular option and what this guide walks through. Download VSCode free at code.visualstudio.com.

Alternatives: You can also use Cursor or Windsurf — both are editors with AI built-in. The steps are nearly identical; we'll note differences as they come up.
​
​

2. An AI Subscription

  • GitHub Copilot — Included with VSCode. Requires a subscription ($10/mo individual or free for some accounts). Install the "GitHub Copilot" extension from the VSCode Extensions panel.

  • Cursor / Windsurf — AI is built into the editor. Each has its own subscription plan.

Most also include a free plan to get started, but note that they will commonly limit you to less intelligent AI models on the free plan.
​
​

3. A Modern Web Browser

Use Google Chrome, or Microsoft Edge. The Local Edit feature requires a modern browser that supports folder access — Safari and Firefox are not supported for this feature.
​
​

4. A Local Folder

Create an empty folder on your computer where your code files will live during editing. For example: Documents/EncompassCode. You'll point both Encompass and your editor to this folder.
​
​

5. Encompass Permissions

You need access to the Dashboard editor in Encompass. If you don't see the code editor or the "Local Edit" button, ask your admin to grant you the appropriate permissions.

Tip: If you're completely new to all of this, start by just installing VSCode and the Copilot extension. You can be up and running in under 10 minutes.

Watch video on YouTube

Steps

Step-by-Step: Your First Vibe Coding Session

Step 1: Set Up Your Editor

For VSCode + GitHub Copilot (Recommended):

  1. Download and install Visual Studio Code.

  2. Open VSCode. Click the Extensions icon on the left sidebar (it looks like four squares).

  3. Search for "GitHub Copilot" and click Install.

  4. Sign in with your GitHub account when prompted. If you don't have one, create a free account at github.com.

  5. You're ready! You should see a Copilot chat icon in your sidebar.

For Cursor: Download from cursor.com and install. AI is built in — just sign up and you're ready. When Encompass asks you to pick an agent, select "Cursor / Other".

For Windsurf: Download from windsurf.com and install. Same as Cursor — select "Cursor / Other" when prompted in Encompass.

Step 2: Open Your Code Block in Encompass

  1. Navigate to the Dashboard containing the Code Block you want to edit (or create a new one).

  2. Open the Code Block's editor — you'll see tabs for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Tests.

  3. Click the "Local Edit" button in the toolbar.

Step 3: Choose Your AI Agent

A dialog will appear titled "Dashboard Local Editing". You'll see a dropdown to select your coding agent:

  • GitHub Copilot — Choose this if you're using VSCode with Copilot

  • Claude Code — Choose this if you're using the Claude Code CLI tool

  • Gemini CLI — Choose this if you're using Google's Gemini CLI

  • Cursor / Other — Choose this for Cursor, Windsurf, or any other editor

Click Confirm.
​
​

Why does this matter? Each agent looks for its instructions in a different file. Encompass creates the right instruction file for whichever agent you pick, so the AI knows exactly how to work with your code.

Step 4: Select Your Local Folder

  1. Your browser will open a folder picker. Navigate to the empty folder you created (e.g., Documents/EncompassCode, or any folder location you want on your computer).

  2. Click Select Folder.

  3. Your browser will ask to grant read and write access — click Allow. This is required so the browser and your editor can share files.

Encompass will now download your code files into that folder. You'll see files like:

  • Dashboard_123_456.html — Your HTML code

  • Dashboard_123_456.css — Your CSS styles

  • Dashboard_123_456.js — Your JavaScript

  • Dashboard_123_456.test.js — Your test file

  • An instructions file for your AI agent

  • Skill files the AI uses for testing and screenshots

If you've edited this Code Block locally before, Encompass will ask whether to use your existing local files or reload fresh from the server. Choose "Reload" to start fresh, or keep your existing files to continue where you left off.

Step 5: Open the Folder in Your Editor

  1. Open VSCode (or your chosen editor).

  2. Go to File → Open Folder and select the same folder you picked in Step 4.

  3. You should see all the downloaded files in the file explorer on the left.

Step 6: Start Vibe Coding!

Now the fun part. Open the AI chat in your editor and describe what you want to build in plain English.

In VSCode: Open Copilot Chat from the sidebar, then switch to Agent mode (look for a dropdown or toggle at the top of the chat panel — switch from "Ask" or "Edit" to "Agent"). Agent mode lets Copilot read, write, and modify your files autonomously.

In Cursor / Windsurf: Use the built-in AI chat panel. These editors are already in agent mode by default.

Example prompts to try:

  • "Create a sales summary dashboard that shows total revenue, order count, and average order value in card layouts"

  • "Add a bar chart showing monthly sales trends"

  • "Make the layout responsive so it looks good on mobile"

  • "Change the color scheme to use blues and grays"

The AI will read the instruction files that Encompass created, understand the Encompass SDK and Design System, and write code that works within your Code Block.

Step 7: Preview Your Changes

Back in your browser, you'll see a preview panel showing your Code Block rendered live. As the AI writes code in your local files, you can see results by clicking Refresh Preview in the preview toolbar.

The preview toolbar buttons (left to right):

  • Refresh Preview — Reloads the preview with your latest local code

  • Reload Code to Local — Overwrites local files with the web editor version

  • Save Code Changes — Pushes your local code back to the web editor

  • Save & Run Tests — Saves and runs your test suite

  • Close Preview — Ends the local editing session

Step 8: Let the AI Run Tests and Take Screenshots

Your AI agent has two powerful built-in skills:

  • Running Tests: The AI can run your Code Block's test suite by writing a small signal file. Encompass picks it up within a few seconds, runs the tests in the real browser environment (with full access to the Encompass SDK), and returns detailed results — including pass/fail status, code coverage percentage, and specific line-by-line coverage data. The AI reads these results and fixes any issues automatically.
    ​
    ​

  • Taking Screenshots: The AI can also request a screenshot of the live preview. Encompass captures the rendered output and saves it as an image file that the AI can see. This lets the AI visually verify layouts, fix alignment issues, and refine the design — all without you having to describe what's wrong.
    ​
    ​

Important: Tests run in the browser, not on your computer. The AI should never try to run npm test or other local test commands — it won't work. The instruction files Encompass created already explain this to your AI agent.

Step 9: Save Your Work

When you're happy with the result:

  1. Click Save Code Changes in the preview toolbar to push your local code back into the Encompass web editor.

  2. Review the code in the web editor if you'd like.

  3. Save and publish your Code Block through the normal Encompass workflow.

Step 10: Iterate and Improve

Vibe coding is iterative. Don't try to describe everything in one prompt. Instead:

  1. Start with the basic structure and layout.

  2. Ask the AI to add features one at a time.

  3. Use screenshots and tests to verify each change.

  4. Refine the design and behavior as you go.

You can come back to Local Edit any time to make changes — your previous files will still be in your local folder, and Encompass will ask if you want to continue from where you left off.

Fields And Definitions

Key Terms and Concepts

Term

What It Means

Vibe Coding

Describing what you want in plain English and letting an AI agent write the code for you. You guide the direction; the AI handles the technical details.

Code Block

An Encompass Dashboard item that contains custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This is what you're building when you vibe code.

Local Edit

The feature that downloads your Code Block files to your computer so you can edit them with an AI-powered editor instead of the built-in web editor.

AI Agent

Software that can read, write, and modify code files on your behalf. Examples: GitHub Copilot (in Agent mode), Cursor's AI, Claude Code.

Agent Mode

A setting in VSCode's Copilot that allows it to autonomously edit files (not just suggest). You must switch to Agent mode for vibe coding to work.

Prompt

The plain English instruction you type to tell the AI what to build or change. Better prompts give better results.

Skills

Built-in capabilities that Encompass gives your AI agent. Currently: test-runner (run unit tests), screenshot (capture the visual preview), and unit-test-writer (guidance for writing tests).

Commands Folder

A folder created in your local directory where the AI agent and browser communicate. The AI writes command files; the browser reads them, executes the action, and writes result files back.

Preview Panel

The live-rendered view of your Code Block shown in the browser during Local Edit. Updates when you click Refresh or when tests/screenshots are triggered.

Instruction File

A file Encompass generates (e.g., copilot-instructions.md or CLAUDE.md) that teaches your AI agent about the Encompass SDK, design system, and how to use the test/screenshot skills.

Code Coverage

A percentage showing how much of your JavaScript code is exercised by your tests. Higher coverage means more of your code has been verified to work correctly.

Encompass SDK

The built-in JavaScript library available in Code Blocks. It provides functions for calling APIs, formatting data, and interacting with other parts of Encompass.

Best Practices

Best Practices for Vibe Coding
​
​

Start Simple, Build Up - Don't try to describe your entire vision in one massive prompt. Start with the basic structure — "Create a page with a header and three data cards" — then layer on complexity in follow-up prompts. This gives you more control and makes it easier for the AI to get things right.

Be Specific in Your Prompts - Instead of "make it look better," try "increase the font size of the header to 24px, add 16px padding around each card, and use a light gray background." The more specific you are, the more accurate the result.

Use Screenshots Often - Let the AI take screenshots frequently so it can see what the page actually looks like. This is especially useful for layout and styling work. After asking for visual changes, tell the AI to take a screenshot and verify the result. If something doesn't look right, just describe the issue and ask it to fix it. You can even take your own screenshots, draw on them what you want, and pass those into your AI coding agent directly in its chat (drag and drop it in).

Let the AI Write and Run Tests - Tests catch bugs early. Ask the AI to write tests for your logic and run them regularly. Aim for at least 80% code coverage — the AI can see coverage results and will add more tests to fill gaps if you ask it to.

Use the Encompass Design System - Your AI agent's instruction file includes the Encompass Design System documentation. Ask it to use Design System components and styles — this ensures your Code Block looks consistent with the rest of Encompass. For example: "Use the Design System card component for the layout."

Don't Fight the AI — Guide It - If the AI goes in a direction you don't like, don't try to micro-manage every line. Instead, explain the overall direction: "I want a cleaner, more minimal look" or "This should be a data table, not a list of cards." Let the AI figure out the implementation details.

Save Frequently - Click Save Code Changes periodically to push your local code back to Encompass. This protects your work and lets you see it in the full Encompass environment, not just the preview panel.

One Feature at a Time - After each new feature or change, take a screenshot, run tests, and verify everything works before moving on. It's much easier to fix issues when you know exactly which change caused them.

Keep the Browser Tab Open - The preview panel must stay open in your browser for Local Edit to work. It's what runs your tests, takes screenshots, and syncs your files. If you accidentally close it, just click "Local Edit" again and select the same folder — Encompass will reconnect to your existing files. If you think it has disconnected from local, use the refresh button to reconnect it; you will get the permission pop-ups from the browser again if it was disconnected.
16989754:
Distributor steps in Encompass for removing a journal entry transaction that Auto-Match wrongly matched on a Bank Reconciliation's Imported tab so the rec balances. Requires v25.11+ and bank rec edit permission.

Minimum Version Required: 25.11

Pre-Conditions

  • Must be attempting to balance or edit an existing Bank Reconciliation.
    ​
    ​

  • The system user must have the necessary permissions to edit Bank Reconciliations and access the Imported tab.
    ​
    ​

  • The unexpected Journal Entry Transaction (JET) and the Bank Reconciliation Transaction (BRT) must have identical amounts.
    ​
    ​

  • The user must have executed the Auto-Match function on the Bank Reconciliation screen's Imported tab.

Steps

1. Navigate to the Bank Reconciliation: Open and Edit the specific Bank Reconciliation record that is currently showing an unexpected transaction (e.g., Bank Reconciliation ID 272).
​
​2. Access the Imported Tab: Click on the Imported tab within the Bank Reconciliation screen.
​
​3. Locate the Unexpected Transaction: Use the filtering or search function to locate the incorrectly linked Journal Entry Transaction (JET) (e.g., Journal Entry Trans ID 51079). You may need to cross-reference the date or amount.
​
​4. Unselect the Journal Entry Transaction: Uncheck or unselect the checkbox/toggle associated with the unexpected Journal Entry Transaction (JET). This action manually breaks the link created by the 'Auto-Match' function.
​
​5. Save the Changes: Click the Save button on the Bank Reconciliation screen to apply the change and remove the JET from the reconciliation.
​
​6. Verify the Balance: Confirm that removing the incorrect JET has corrected the balance of the Bank Reconciliation and proceed with the rest of the balancing process.

Fields And Definitions

  • Bank Reconciliation (BR): The process of verifying that the bank statement balance agrees with the cash balance on a company's general ledger.

  • Journal Entry (JE): A record of a financial transaction in an accounting system.

  • Journal Entry Transaction: A specific line item/debit/credit within a broader Journal Entry.

    • Example: Journal Entry Trans ID 51079.

  • Bank Reconciliation Transaction (BRT): A transaction record imported from a bank statement (e.g., via a file import) that is being matched against a JET.

    • Example: Bank Rec Trans ID 12709.

  • Auto-Match: A feature within the Bank Reconciliation screen's Imported tab that automatically links unreconciled Bank Reconciliation Transactions to Journal Entry Transactions based on a specific, priority-based logic:

    1. Priority 3 (Highest): Match by Check Number.

    2. Priority 2: Match by Date.

    3. Priority 1 (Lowest): Match by Amount Only.

  • Import Routine: A scheduled or manually run process that uploads and inserts external data (like bank statement files) into the system for use in reconciliation.

Best Practices

16989755:
Distributor reference for the Date Conversions table in Encompass used in reports: week numbering (setting 3431), business days (setting 341), trimesters and selling days. Requires v26.02+; admin to change.

Minimum Version Required: 26.02

Pre-Conditions

  • Administration: To adjust calculation logic (such as Week Numbering or Business Day definitions), the user must be a System Administrator with access to System Settings.

Steps

Overview
​
​The Date Conversions table serves as the system's central calendar reference. It is automatically populated by the system (up to 10 years in advance) and is primarily used as a data source for Reports to aggregate data by specific timeframes (e.g., Trimester, Fiscal Week, or Selling Day).

Viewing Date Conversion Data
​
​To validate current date logic or look up specific conversion values:

  1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Date Conversions table.
    ​
    ​

  2. Review the columns to understand how a specific Date maps to a Week, Quarter, or Business Day status.

Configuring Week Numbering (Setting 3431)
​
​

  • The specific method used to calculate "Week" and "Day of Week" is controlled by System Setting 3431.
    ​
    ​

  • This setting resolves discrepancies between different global standards (e.g., Excel vs. ISO).

Option 0: ISO 8601 (International Standard)
​
​

  1. First Day of Week: Monday.
    ​
    ​

  2. Week 1 Definition: The first week of the year is the week that contains January 4th (or the first week with at least 4 days in the new year).
    ​
    ​

  3. Behavior: This is the international business standard. It avoids split weeks but can result in the first few days of January falling into the last week of the previous year's numbering.
    ​
    ​

  4. Learn More: ISO 8601 Week Dates (Wikipedia)
    ​
    ​
    ​
    ​

Option 1: North American / Excel Standard
​
​

  1. First Day of Week: Sunday.
    ​
    ​

  2. Week 1 Definition: The first week of the year is the week that contains January 1st.
    ​
    ​

  3. Behavior: This aligns with standard US calendars and Microsoft Excel's default "System 1" week numbering. It ensures that January 1st is always in Week 1.
    ​
    ​

  4. Learn More: Week Numbering Systems (Excel Functions)
    ​
    ​

Note: Changing this setting will update the Week, DayOfWeek, YearWeek, and YearQuarter columns during the next weekly recalculation.

Configuring Business Days (Setting 341)
​
​

The Is Business Day column is calculated based on System Setting 341.
​
This determines which weekend days are considered working days:

  • 0: No weekend business (Monday-Friday only).
    ​
    ​

  • 1: Saturday is a business day.
    ​
    ​

  • 2: Sunday is a business day.
    ​
    ​

  • 3: Both Saturday and Sunday are business days.

Using Date Conversions in Reporting
​
​When building custom reports, join the Date Conversions table to your transaction table (e.g., Sales or Inventory) using the Date column.
​
​

  • Example: To create a report showing "Sales by Trimester," join your Sales table to Date Conversions, and group your results by the Trimester column.

Fields And Definitions

  • Date: The standard calendar date (Primary Key).
    ​
    ​

  • Is Business Day: A boolean flag (1 or 0) indicating if the date is a working day based on System Setting 341.
    ​
    ​

  • Week: The week number (1-53) of the year. The calculation (Monday-start vs. Sunday-start) depends on Setting 3431.
    ​
    ​

  • Day Of Week: The numeric day of the week. If using ISO 8601, Monday = 1. If using North American, Sunday = 1.
    ​
    ​

  • Trimester: Breaks the year into three fixed 4-month periods... 1: January - April; 2: May - August; 3: September - December
    ​
    ​

  • Selling Day of Month: A sequential counter of Business Days within a specific month. (e.g., If the 1st is a Sunday and non-business, the 2nd (Monday) is Selling Day 1).
    ​
    ​

  • Phase: Represents a 4-week cycle calculation used for specific delivery or inventory rotations.
    ​
    ​

  • Forecast Year / Forecast Week: These columns are calculated based on Setting 56 (Weekly Forecast Start Date) and allow for forecasting logic that differs from the standard calendar week.

Best Practices

  • Consistency is Key: Avoid changing Setting 3431 (Week Mode) in the middle of a fiscal year, as this can cause reporting discontinuities (e.g., data shifting from Week 10 to Week 11 unexpectedly).

  4. Once registration is successful, the popup will close, and your passkey will be active.

16989759:
Distributor steps for DSDLink orders landing in Import Conflicts or on a later delivery date in Encompass: check cut-off times, locked load sheets and Routing Method 2 logic. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • DSDLink Integration: Active account for customer order submissions.

  • Routing Configuration: Exchange Configuration set to Routing Method 2: Next Scheduled Delivery Event Then Stop.

  • Cut-off Times: Defined "Order Cut-Off Times" in Route Types (e.g., 4:00 PM).

  • Permissions: User access to the Import Conflicts dashboard and Invoice Audit records.

Steps

  1. Identify the Conflict: Navigate to the Import Conflicts dashboard and locate the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  2. Verify the Submission Timestamp: Open the Invoice Audit. Compare the "Date Added" against your Route Type cut-off time.
    ​
    ​

  3. Check Load Sheet Status: Check the Field Audit for the intended delivery date. If the Load Sheet was "Locked for Routing" (by a user or Auto_Lock_LoadSheets) before the invoice arrived, the "Push" logic was triggered.
    ​
    ​

  4. Review the PO Date: Check the raw 850 file for the PODate. The dashboard often displays this requested date, even if the system attempted to find a different stop based on routing rules.
    ​
    ​

  5. Contact Support if Unresolved: If the target date does not align with the customer's schedule, contact support with the following:
    ​
    ​

    • Invoice Audit ID and Customer ID.
      ​
      ​

    • Exact Error Message (e.g., "Problem 5: Order cut-off time passed").
      ​
      ​

    • Timestamp of order submission vs. your system's cut-off.
      ​
      ​

    • Exchange Task ID.

Fields And Definitions

In an Exchange Configuration using Routing Method 2, the software validates the order date against your routing schedule and warehouse status.
​
​

How the Logic Works

  1. The Start Point: Regardless of the date the customer selects in DSDLink (PODate), the system resets its search starting point to Today + 1 (tomorrow).
    ​
    ​

  2. The Cut-off/Lock Check: The system checks the Route Type cutoff and the Load Sheet status. If the invoice arrives after the cutoff (e.g., 4:01 PM) or the Load Sheet is Locked for Routing, that date is skipped.
    ​
    ​

  3. The Push: The system jumps to the next scheduled stop in the customer's record. This is why an order for "tomorrow" may show a date for "next week" if it was submitted just minutes after the load sheet locked.

  • Routing Method 2: Logic that finds the next valid delivery date based on the customer’s assigned stop schedule, starting from Today + 1.
    ​
    ​

  • Locked for Routing: Status of a Load Sheet meaning that no additional edits can be made while picking and routing is in process. No further invoices can be added without manually unlocking it.
    ​
    ​

  • Import Conflict: A holding area for invoices that cannot be placed on a Load Sheet due to errors or missed cut-offs.
    ​
    ​

  • PODate: The specific delivery date requested by the customer in the DSDLink interface.

Best Practices

  • Align Lock Times: Coordinate your Auto_Lock_LoadSheets schedule with your order cut-off times.
    ​
    ​

  • Monitor Post-Cutoff: Review the Import Conflicts dashboard daily shortly after the cut-off time to manually move orders that missed the window.
    ​
    ​

  • Communicate with Users: Ensure DSDLink users know that even a one-minute delay past the cutoff will push their order to the next scheduled delivery.

Screenshot

Troubleshooting Login Issues

Q: Why is a customer receiving a 'Permission Denied' error when attempting to log in?

A: This typically indicates the user is attempting to log in via an incorrect URL or the initial invitation process was misrouted. Essentially, the system believes the user is logging into a distributor-side (Encompass) account instead of the customer-side (dsdlink) account.

How to Resolve:

  • Verify the URL: Confirm the customer is navigating to dsdlink.com. They may have unintentionally navigated to their distributorship’s Encompass site.
    ​
    ​

  • Confirm the Invitation Method: If an invitation was sent, ensure the sales rep or distributor used the 'Invite to DSDLink' hyperlink on the customer user record, and not the general 'Invite User' option (which is for internal Encompass users).
    ​
    ​

  • If the URL is correct and the issue persists: Please create a support ticket. We can verify and update the user's role and permissions directly within the dsdlink system to resolve the error.

Resolving 'Invalid Username or Password' Errors

Q: A customer reports seeing an 'Invalid Username or Password' error when attempting to log in. What should they do?

A: This indicates that the credentials entered do not match a login associated with the email address on file, or no login exists for that email.

How to Resolve:

  • Advise Email Login: Instruct the customer to use their email address as the primary login method (this is the advised standard, even though usernames are technically valid).
    ​
    ​

  • Clear Saved Credentials: Ask the customer to confirm they do not have an incorrect password saved in their browser's autofill feature.
    ​
    ​

  • Initiate Password Reset: If the password is forgotten, they must use the 'Forgot Password' link on the dsdlink login page to reset it themselves.
    ​
    ​

  • When to Escalate: Support does not have visibility beyond these self-service steps. If the issue persists, please walk through the process with the retailer to gather specific screenshots or details before submitting a support ticket.

Password Reset Email Not Received

Q: A customer is not receiving the password reset email. What is the likely cause?

A: This typically occurs because the email is being flagged as spam or the user's system is blocking the sender. In some cases, the email system may have filed a 'complaint,' which causes future password reset emails to fail delivery.

How to Resolve:

  • Check Spam and Whitelist: Instruct the customer to confirm their email address and immediately check their junk/spam folder. Advise them to whitelist the dsdlink sending address, [email protected].
    ​
    ​

  • Utilize Mobile Reset: If the email does not arrive, they must use the 'Mobile' option from the dropdown menu on the password reset page. This allows them to receive the password reset link securely via a text message to their verified mobile number, bypassing any email server issues. If the user does not have a mobile number added to their account, create a ticket for support and we can add a mobile number and send the initial text reset.

Resolving Incorrect Business Information

Q: A customer reports seeing incorrect or outdated business information.

A: This occurs because the retail business name was changed outside of dsdlink after the initial Global Customer record was created. Since dsdlink utilizes this single record across all distributors, name changes must be manually updated within the dsdlink system to ensure accuracy.

How to Resolve:

Two parties can update this information:

  • Distributor Action: A distributor user with the "Distributor IT contact" permission must update the customer name directly from the User Management dashboard.
    ​
    ​

  • Retailer Action: The retailer can navigate to their Manage dashboard and update the business name themselves using the "Business" tab.

Managing Users and Account Information

Q: How can a customer remove old users from their account or change the name/email address associated with their profile?

A: Retailers can manage their individual profile information and remove old users via the dsdlink User Management Dashboard (if they possess the 3) Retailer Role 2 + User Management).

How to Resolve:

  • Update Name/Email: To update their name or email address, the user must click on their name when logged in, navigate to "Profile," and make adjustments there.
    ​
    ​

  • Addressing Email Conflicts: Note that a user's email address may not be updated if it currently exists in other distributor databases. If this conflict occurs, the user must create a new account with the correct email address and then link it to the business manually or via a new invitation from your site.
    ​
    ​

  • Removing Users: Users with the Main Role can remove or modify access for old employees directly from the User Management Dashboard (Manage tab).

Resolving Product Visibility Issues

Q: Why is a customer seeing (or not seeing) specific products in dsdlink?

A: Product visibility is controlled entirely by the distributor. Customers are only permitted to view products that the distributor has explicitly designated to their account via the Product Control Settings within the Encompass system (e.g., specific product groups, allocations, or distribution areas).

How to Resolve:

  • Verify Distributor Controls: A distributor user must check the product controls in Encompass to confirm the customer's settings are accurately configured for the expected product visibility. Please note, if any changes were made to product controls, there is a timing delay to reflect changes in dsdlink. Please account for about 3 hours for changes to reflect.
    ​
    ​

  • Escalation Protocol: If the customer and product controls appear correctly set up and the visibility remains inaccurate in dsdlink, you must gather the Customer ID and Product ID to create a support ticket for further investigation.

16989768:
Video plus steps for distributors handling keg deposits in Encompass: GL setup for full and empty kegs, buying kegs with third-party deposits (e.g. MicroStar), returning empties and partial keg returns. Requires v24.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 24.01

Watch video on YouTube

Steps

Managing the Keg Deposits Workflow

Part 1: Key Concepts and General Ledger Setup
​
​

The Three Rules of Keg Deposits:
​
​

  1. Every keg has a deposit value for the shell. If the supplier isn't charging it, someone is (e.g., a third-party provider).
    ​
    ​

  2. Every empty has an FOB (a value). The value of the empty shell must be equal to the deposit cost charged for the full keg.
    ​
    ​

  3. Not all suppliers charge the same deposit cost. If a supplier's deposit cost is different, you must create a separate empty keg product with a matching FOB.

General Ledger (GL) Best Practice
​
​

To ensure a "purely exchange transaction" (where you neither make nor lose money on the shell), the income and cost accounts for the deposit portion must offset:
​
​

  • Deposit Income Account on the Full Keg product must equal the Income Account on the Empty Keg product.
    ​
    ​

  • Deposit COGS Account on the Full Keg product must equal the COGS Account on the Empty Keg product.
    ​
    ​

This is achieved by mapping all four fields to the same GL account (e.g., a "Customer Keg Deposits" or "Inventory Asset" account).

Part 2: Workflow for Full Keg Purchase
​

When receiving a full keg, the product is split into two costings: the liquid and the shell deposit.
​
​

Costing Component

Full Keg Product Field

GL Impact

Liquid

FOB Value

Drives COGS (offsets inventory) and Income (where you make margins).

Shell

Deposit Cost

Drives Deposit COGS and Deposit Income (should offset).

Procedure: Purchasing a Full Keg with a Third-Party Deposit
​
​

This procedure accrues the shell value as a payable to the third party (e.g., MicroStar) while ensuring the purchase bill only pays the supplier for the liquid.

Pre-Step: Create a Non-Inventory Product (e.g., "3RD PARTY KEG DEPOSIT") and map its Expense Account to a liability account (e.g., Accrued Payables Miscellaneous).
​
​

  1. Enter the Full Keg: On the purchase document, enter the full keg product and:
    ​
    - Enter the full keg's Deposit amount as if the supplier were charging it (e.g., $30.00).
    ​
    - The FOB is the cost of the liquid only (e.g., $79.00).
    ​
    ​
    ​

  2. Accrue the Payable: Add the Non-Inventory Product (e.g., "3RD PARTY KEG DEPOSIT") as a separate line item:
    ​
    - Enter a Negative Quantity equal to the number of full kegs on the purchase (e.g., 10).
    ​
    - Enter the deposit amount as the FOB for this line (e.g., $30.00).
    ​
    ​
    ​

  3. Bill Amount: The total purchase document value will now equal the liquid's FOB amount (e.g., $790.00), which is the amount you pay the brewery. The deposit value is correctly placed into your inventory and accrued as a liability to the third-party provider.

Part 3: Workflow for Returning Empty KegsProcedure: Returning Empties to a Third-Party Provider (Reconciliation)
​
​

Use this workflow if the third-party provider (e.g., MicroStar) sends a reconciliation statement instead of paying you immediately for the returned empties.
​
​

  1. Enter the Empty Kegs: On the purchase document (return), enter the empty keg product (e.g., "KEG LOGISTICS EMPTY KEG") and:
    ​
    - Enter a Negative Quantity for the number of empties returned (e.g., (10)).
    ​
    - Enter the deposit value as the FOB (e.g., $30.00).
    ​
    ​
    ​

  2. Offset the Accrued Payable: Add the Non-Inventory Product (e.g., "3RD PARTY KEG DEPOSIT") as a separate line item:
    ​
    - Enter a Positive Quantity equal to the number of empties returned (e.g., 10).
    ​
    - Enter the deposit amount as the FOB for this line (e.g., $30.00).
    ​
    ​
    ​

  3. Result: This process debits the Accrued Payables (liability) and credits the Brewery Keg Deposits (asset), making your accrued payables balance match the third party's reconciliation.

Best Practice: Matching Deposit Costs
​
​

  • Separate Empty Products: If Supplier A charges a $30 deposit and Supplier B charges a $40 deposit, you must create two empty keg products:
    ​
    Empty Keg A: FOB = $30.00
    ​
    Empty Keg B: FOB = $40.00
    ​
    ​

  • Warehouse Separation: The solution to managing these different empty products is to separate them by supplier in the warehouse on return and perform periodic physical counts to ensure correct assignment and valuation.

Part 4: Workflow for Partial Keg Returns from a Retailer
​
​

This workflow ensures the retailer is refunded for the partial liquid and the full deposit on the shell.
​
​

Pre-Step: For the full keg product, ensure Consumable Units Per Case is set to a value greater than one (e.g., 4) to allow for fractional returns.
​
​

  1. Enter the Partial Liquid Return: On the return document, enter the full keg product as a decimal or fractional unit to reflect the liquid volume being returned (e.g., (0.5) or (2/4)).
    ​
    ​Result: The retailer is refunded the price for the returned liquid portion.
    ​
    ​
    ​

  2. Enter the Empty Shell Return: Add the corresponding Empty Shell Product (e.g., "EMPTY 1/2 BBL") with a quantity of (1).
    ​
    ​Result: The retailer is refunded the full deposit for the shell.
    ​
    ​
    ​

  3. Inventory Adjustment: After the return, adjust the partial keg out of inventory (e.g., for office use or disposal) since you won't be selling a partial keg.

Part 5: Call to Action
​
​

To ensure you're is using these best practices, perform the following reviews:
​
​

  1. Review Full Keg Products:
    ​
    - Check your Inventory Table or run an Inventory Depletions Report (value = Deposit) to confirm the Deposit Value is correct for every full keg product.
    ​
    ​
    ​

  2. Review Empty Products:
    ​
    - Check your Inventories Table or run an Inventory Valuation Report (value = FOB or Landed Cost) to confirm the FOB for each empty shell product matches its corresponding full keg's deposit cost.
    ​
    - If the quantity does not match the sum of the deposit or FOB value, set the report to show FIFO layers to investigate discrepancies causing FIFO adjustments.
    ​
    ​
    ​

  3. Review Third-Party Provider Processes:
    ​
    - Confirm your process for accounting for third-party deposits (e.g., MicroStar, Kegspediter) to ensure it aligns with the purchasing and return procedures outlined above.
