16989965:
Explains the daily email sending limit in Encompass: how it is calculated from system size (minimum 1,000/day) and why emails may be blocked or delayed once it is reached. Requires v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Steps

Encompass includes a built-in limit on the total number of emails that can be sent from the system each day. This limit helps ensure system stability and manage email sending resources effectively.

  • The daily email limit is calculated automatically based on a variety of size calculations of your Encompass system, based on number of routes, customers, subscription amount, etc. This ensures that larger systems have a larger limit.
    ​
    ​

  • There is also a minimum guaranteed limit of 1,000 emails, even for the smallest system.
    ​
    ​

  • The actual limit applied for the day is the higher value between the calculated limit and the relevant minimum threshold (1,000 or 20,000).
    ​

  • The system tracks the number of emails sent throughout the day, comparing it against this calculated daily limit.
    ​
    ​

  • If the number of emails attempted to be sent exceeds the daily limit, further email sending may be blocked or delayed until the limit resets the following day.
    ​

  • These limits are in place due to restrictions to prevent Spam proliferation.
16989966:
Reference for the InvoiceTransAddProduct EDBL import in Encompass: bulk-add product lines to existing or new invoices with pricing, promotions, charges and payments. Needs InvoiceEdit permission; v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You must have the InvoiceEdit permission to use this routine.

  • Products must already exist in the system before importing.

  • Customers must already exist in the system before importing.

  • If you plan to use LocationID_Translation, the locations must already exist.

  • If you plan to use PromotionID, the promotions must already exist.

  • If you plan to use PaymentTypeID, the payment types must already exist.

Steps

The InvoiceTransAddProduct routine allows you to add products (line items) to invoices. It can either add products to existing invoices or create new invoices when needed.

This routine will:

Match imported data to existing invoices using various methods:

  • Direct match by InvoiceID (if provided)

  • Match by CustomerID + PONum combination

  • Match by CustomerID + InvoiceNum combination

  • Match by CustomerID + TranslationInvoiceNum

Create new invoices if needed (when in Add or Update+Add mode) when no matching invoice is found.

Add or update invoice transactions (line items) with product and pricing information.

Handle currency conversion if specified.

Calculate pricing based on unit price, full price, and discounts.

Apply promotions if specified.

The behavior changes based on the import action selected:

  • Add Only: Only creates new invoice transactions, skips existing ones.

  • Update Only: Only updates existing invoice transactions, doesn't create new ones.

  • Update or Add: Updates existing transactions when found, creates new ones when not found.

Fields And Definitions

Invoice Identification Fields:

  • InvoiceID - The internal ID of an existing invoice to update (optional).

  • InvoiceNum - The invoice number displayed to users.

  • TranslationInvoiceNum - External system's invoice ID for cross-reference.

  • PONum - Purchase order number from customer.

Customer and Location Information:

  • CustomerID - Internal ID of the customer for this invoice.

  • CustomerID_Translation - External system's customer ID for matching.

  • LocationID - Internal ID of the location for this invoice (defaults to user's location).

  • LocationID_Translation - External system's location ID for matching.

Date and Scheduling:

  • Date - The invoice date (defaults to next business day).

  • DueDate - Due date for payment.

  • LoadSheetID - Links invoice to a specific load sheet for delivery.

  • RouteID - Internal ID of the delivery route.

  • RouteNum - Route number for delivery.

Product Information:

  • ProductID - Internal ID of the product being added.

  • ProductID_Translation - External system's product ID for matching.

  • ProductName - Name of the product (overrides default if provided).

  • NumUnits - Number of individual units of the product.

  • NumUnitsCases - Number of cases of the product (converts to units automatically).

Pricing Information:

  • FullPrice - Original price before discounts (per unit).

  • UnitPrice - Price after discounts (per unit).

  • Discount - Primary discount amount (per unit).

  • Discount2 - Secondary discount amount (per unit).

  • Deposit - Container deposit amount (per unit).

  • AutoCalculateMethod - Controls how pricing is calculated.

  • PromoOverridden - Indicates if promotion pricing is overridden.

Promotion Information:

  • PromotionID - Internal ID of the primary promotion applied.

  • PromotionID2 - Internal ID of the secondary promotion applied.

  • Participation - Primary manufacturer participation amount.

  • Participation2 - Secondary manufacturer participation amount.

Invoice Charges:

  • InvoiceCharge1 to InvoiceCharge5 - Additional charge amounts.

  • InvoiceChargeType1 to InvoiceChargeType5 - Types of additional charges.

Payment Information:

  • Receipt - Payment amount received.

  • PaymentTypeID - Internal ID of the payment method.

  • PaymentTypeID_Translation - External system's payment type ID.

Additional Fields:

  • Memo - Notes on the invoice.

  • Locked - Whether the invoice should be locked against changes.

  • DeliveryUserName - Username of the delivery person.

  • EntrySource - Source system for the entry.

  • AllocationID - Links to inventory allocation.

  • JobID - Links to a job.

  • TransSource - Source of the transaction.

  • TransNote - Note for this transaction.

  • ClearAllTrans - If set to 1, zeroes quantities for products not in import.

  • ReasonID - Reason code (for returns, etc.).

Currency Handling:

  • CurrencyID - Internal ID of the currency used.

  • CurrencyID_Translation - External system's currency ID.

  • ExchangeRate - Exchange rate for currency conversion.

Purchase Transaction Linkage:

  • PurchaseTransID - Links to a purchase transaction.

  • PurchaseTransIDLocked - Controls whether the purchase transaction link can be changed.

Best Practices

Matching Existing Invoices:

  • Provide either InvoiceID, PONum, InvoiceNum, or TranslationInvoiceNum to match to existing invoices.

  • For best results, ensure CustomerID is always included.

Creating New Invoices:

  • When creating new invoices, provide Date, CustomerID, and either RouteID or RouteNum.

  • Including a PONum or InvoiceNum helps with future identification.

Product Quantities:

  • You can provide either NumUnits or NumUnitsCases - the system will convert cases to units automatically.

  • Always ensure ProductID or ProductID_Translation is correctly mapped.

Pricing Options:

  • You need to provide either FullPrice and Discount, or just UnitPrice.

  • If you provide UnitPrice and FullPrice, Discount will be calculated automatically.

Bulk Updates:

  • Use ClearAllTrans=1 to set quantity to zero for line items that aren't in your import file.

  • This is useful for importing the complete state of an invoice.

Performance:

  • Import related records in batches of 5,000 or fewer for optimal performance.

  • For large imports, consider scheduling during off-peak hours.

Currency Handling:

  • If using foreign currency, always provide both CurrencyID and ExchangeRate.

  • All price values are stored in your system's base currency but displayed in the invoice's currency.

Common Issues:

  • If products aren't appearing, check that the ProductID exists in your system.

  • If invoices are created but no line items appear, verify that both CustomerID and ProductID are valid.

  • For discounts to apply correctly, both PromotionID and Discount fields must be properly set.
16989967:
Distributor guide to the Wholesale Units per Case (WUPC) conversion tool: Correction3 bin adjustments, moving stock back via BinTransEDBL, and fixing PromotionsProducts pricing. Needs All Locations on user; v25.06+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.06

Pre-Conditions

  • The system setting "Enter Promotion Discounts and Product Prices by Case Values" must be set to true. This is set to true to allow the system to calculate the unit price as expected after the tool is updated. Once completing the process, you can set this back to false.
    ​
    ​

  • A default Correction3 bin should be configured in your system to catch system corrections.
    ​
    ​

  • The Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories scheduled task runs, typically early Sunday morning.
    ​
    ​

  • Access to import routines for mass product moves (e.g., BinTransEDBL import routine) if necessary.
    ​
    ​

  • Understanding of package configurations and their impact on wholesale units.
    ​
    ​

  • Users must have All Locations set to TRUE on their User Record to run the tool.

Steps

1. Understand WUPC Conversion Impact: When the WUPC is changed for a product (e.g., from 1 unit per case to 12 units per case), the system treats the original inventory in units as now equating to a different number of cases. This difference is what triggers the product to be moved to an adjustment bin. This is expected behavior.
​
2. Verify Correction3 Bin Configuration: Ensure you have a dedicated "Correction3 bin" set up. This bin should be named clearly (e.g., "Correction3 bin") and ideally configured as a back stock bin to prevent pickers from being prompted to pick from it. This bin will temporarily hold inventory adjusted by the Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories scheduled task.
​
​3. Allow for Scheduled Task Execution: The Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories scheduled task is responsible for processing inventory corrections related to WUPC changes. This task typically runs early Sunday morning. It is highly recommended to perform WUPC conversions on a Friday evening to allow this task to run over the weekend.
​
​4. Monitor the Correction3 Bin: After the Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories task has run, check your designated Correction3 bin. Any inventory adjustments resulting from the WUPC conversion will appear in this bin.
​
5. Move Product from Adjustment Bin to Original Bin:

  • Manual Move: For smaller quantities, manually move the products from the Correction3 bin back to their original pickable bins within the system.

  • Mass Import (Recommended for Large Quantities): If you are comfortable with import routines, create a BinTransEDBL import routine. This file will require two lines per product:

    • A negative transaction to deplete the Correction3 bin.

    • A positive transaction to increase the inventory in the product's pickable bin.


​6. Address Pricing Discrepancies:

  • Understand Pricing Logic: When WUPC changes, the system's InvoicingTrigger_Set_CaseAmountAndLineAggs logic may re-calculate PromotionsProducts amounts based on the new WUPC. If the system's pricing calculations are incorrect (e.g., multiplying by units instead of dividing), you will need to adjust.

  • Update Pricing via Table Import: Pricing can be updated efficiently using a table import for the PromotionsProducts table. This allows you to bulk update the Amount and Case Amount values to ensure they calculate correctly with the new WUPC.

  • Wait for Scheduled Task: After updating pricing via import, wait for the Recalculate_Invoice_Pricing scheduled task to run; this will apply the changes to your invoice data.

Fields And Definitions

  • WUPC (Wholesale Units Per Case): The number of individual units (e.g., bottles, cans) contained within one wholesale case of a product. Changing this value affects how inventory is tracked and priced.
    ​
    ​

  • Adjustment Bin: A designated bin in the inventory system where products are temporarily moved due to discrepancies or system adjustments (like those after a WUPC conversion). Products in this bin are typically considered unsellable until reconciled.
    ​
    ​

  • Correction3 Bin: A user-defined default bin specifically configured to catch system-generated inventory corrections, often resulting from scheduled tasks like Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories.
    ​
    ​

  • Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories (Scheduled Task): An automated process that runs periodically to reconcile and adjust bin inventories based on system logic, including changes from WUPC conversions. This task is crucial for moving adjusted inventory to the Correction3 bin.
    ​
    ​

  • Recalculate_Invoice_Pricing (Scheduled Task): An automated process that recalculates pricing on invoices, ensuring that changes made to product pricing (e.g., via PromotionsProducts updates) are correctly reflected.
    ​
    ​

  • PromotionsProducts: A system table or module where product pricing details are stored and managed, including case amounts and unit amounts.
    ​
    ​

  • BinTransEDBL: An import routine within the system that allows for the mass import of bin transfer transactions, enabling efficient movement of products between bins.
    ​
    ​

  • Back Stock Bin: A type of inventory bin typically used for overflow or bulk storage, designed so that pickers are not prompted to pick from it directly. This is recommended for Correction3 bins.

Best Practices

  • Perform WUPC Conversions on Weekends or on Friday Afternoon: Always plan to run the WUPC conversion tool on a Friday evening. This allows the Correct_BinInventories_2_Inventories scheduled task to run over the weekend, minimizing disruption to your busiest operational days.
    ​
    ​

  • Configure Pricing Calculation Setting: Ensure the system setting "Enter Promotion Discounts and Product Prices by Case Values" is set to true during the WUPC conversion process to allow for accurate unit price calculation. This setting can be reverted to false once the conversion and associated pricing adjustments are complete.
    ​
    ​

  • Test in a Non-Production Environment: Before implementing any WUPC changes on your live site, thoroughly test the entire conversion and adjustment process in a dedicated test environment. This helps identify and resolve potential issues without impacting your day-to-day operations.
    ​
    ​

  • Proactive Bin Management: Create and clearly label a dedicated default Correction3 bin. The Default Correction3 Bin (set on the Default Bins table) needs to be a back stock bin type. This prevents it from being a pick location and makes it easier to manage inventory moved there.
    ​
    ​

  • In the event of a Correction3 bin transaction after the WUPC tool has been run, count your inventory and adjust cases as needed.
    ​
    ​

  • Understand System Logic: Be aware that WUPC changes are a significant endeavor and inherently involve inventory adjustments due to the change in how units are accounted for within a case. Inventory is the sum of Units; if the Unit value changes on for a product, the associated inventory will need to be confirmed.
    ​
    ​

  • Utilize Import Routines: For large-scale WUPC conversions, familiarize yourself with and leverage system import routines (e.g., BinTransEDBL) to mass move products and update pricing. This significantly reduces manual effort.
    ​
    ​

  • Review Documentation: Regularly consult the updated help resources for the WUPC tool, which should include detailed steps for managing bin inventories and updating pricing after a conversion.

16989969:
Distributor steps in Encompass for fixing a purchase posting to the wrong expense account for non-inventory products by checking Expense Account Maps and correcting the purchase or with a JE. Requires v25.04+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.04

Pre-Conditions

  • You have identified a Purchase where the Purchase Accounts reflect an incorrect expense account for a non-inventory product.
    ​
    ​

  • You have access to the system's Expense Account Maps table.
    ​
    ​

  • You have the necessary permissions to view and potentially edit this table.

Steps

  1. Navigate to the Expense Account Maps Table:
    ​
    ​

    • Use the universal search functionality within the system.
      ​
      ​

    • Search for "Expense Account Maps" and select the corresponding table.
      ​
      ​

  2. Identify the Product and Location on the Purchase:
    ​
    ​

    • Note the specific non-inventory Product that is showing the incorrect expense account on the Purchase.
      ​
      ​

    • Note the Company and Location associated with the Purchase.
      ​
      ​

  3. Locate the Relevant Expense Account Map Record(s):
    ​
    ​

    • Within the Expense Account Maps table, look for records that match the following criteria:
      ​
      ​

      • Product: Does a map exist for the specific Product?
        ​
        ​

      • Product Type: (Implicit based on being a non-inventory product)
        ​
        ​

      • Location: Does a map exist for the specific Location of the Purchase?
        ​
        ​

      • Company: Does a map exist for the specific Company of the Purchase?
        ​
        ​

    • The system may use a combination of these fields to determine the applicable Expense Account Map. Check for the most specific match first (Product, Location, Company), then less specific (Product, Company), (Product, Location), (Location, Company), (Product only), (Location only), or a default (Company only).
      ​
      ​

  4. Verify the Expense Account:
    ​
    ​

    • Once the relevant Expense Account Map record(s) is located, examine the Expense Account field.
      ​
      ​

    • Ensure that the GL account listed in this field is the correct expense account that should be associated with the Product for the given Company and Location (or the applicable combination).
      ​
      ​

    • If the Expense Account is incorrect, note the incorrect account and the correct account.
      ​
      ​

  5. Correct the Expense Account Map (If Necessary and if you have permissions):
    ​
    ​

    • If the Expense Account in the Expense Account Map is incorrect, update it to the correct GL account.
      ​
      ​

  6. Address Purchases with Incorrect Accounts:
    ​
    ​

    • If the Purchase is in Verified Status and the AP Close Date can be rolled back:
      ​
      ​

      • Roll back the AP Close Date.
        ​
        ​

      • Un-verify the Purchase.
        ​
        ​

      • Edit and save the Purchase document (this should trigger a recalculation of the Purchase Accounts based on the updated Expense Account Map).
        ​
        ​

      • Verify the Purchase again.
        ​
        ​

    • If too much time has passed to roll back the AP Close Date:
      ​
      ​

      • Option 1: Reverse and Recreate:
        ​
        ​

        • Reverse the incorrect Purchase.
          ​
          ​

        • Verify the reversal.
          ​
          ​

        • Make the necessary corrections to the Expense Account Maps.
          ​
          ​

        • Recreate the Purchase with the correct information.
          ​
          ​

      • Option 2: Journal Entry Correction:

        • Make the necessary corrections to the Expense Account Maps.
          ​
          ​

        • Create a simple journal entry to transfer the balance from the incorrect expense account to the correct expense account for the historical Purchase.
          ​
          ​

  7. Investigate Further if the Issue Persists:
    ​
    ​

    • If the Expense Account Maps appear to be configured correctly, there might be other system settings or product configurations influencing the Purchase Accounts.
      ​
      ​

    • Review the product setup and any relevant purchasing rules.

Fields And Definitions

  • Expense Account Maps: A table in the system that links non-inventory Products to specific General Ledger Expense Accounts for Purchases.
    ​
    ​

  • Company: The specific company or legal entity within the system to which this Expense Account Map applies.
    ​
    ​

  • Location: The specific location within the company to which this Expense Account Map applies.
    ​
    ​

  • Product: The specific non-inventory product being mapped to an expense account.
    ​
    ​

  • Expense Account: The General Ledger account that the value of the mapped Product will be assigned to on Purchase Accounts.
    ​
    ​

  • Purchase Accounts: The set of accounting entries (similar to a journal entry) created when a Purchase Order is processed. These reflect the impact of the purchase on various GL accounts.
    ​
    ​

  • Verified Status: A status in the system indicating that a Purchase has been finalized and may have downstream financial implications.
    ​
    ​

  • AP Close Date: A date that signifies the end of an Accounts Payable period, often restricting changes to transactions before that date.
    ​
    ​

  • Roll Back: The action of moving the AP Close Date backward, allowing modifications to prior periods.
    ​
    ​

  • Un-verify: The action of reverting a Purchase from a Verified status, allowing edits.
    ​
    ​

  • Reverse Purchase: Creating a transaction that negates the financial impact of the original Purchase.

Best Practices

  • Establish clear rules for how Expense Account Maps should be created based on Product, Location, and Company.
    ​
    ​

  • Regularly review Expense Account Maps, especially when new non-inventory products are added or GL accounts change.
    ​
    ​

  • Consider using specific Product mappings over more general Location or Company mappings for greater accuracy.
    ​
    ​

  • Train users on the importance of verifying Purchase Accounts before verifying Purchases.

    ​

  • If the Undeposited Account is incorrect, note the incorrect account and the correct account.
    ​
    ​

5. Verify the Deposit Error Account:

  • In the same Deposit Account Map record, examine the Deposit Error Account field.
    ​
    ​

  • Ensure that the GL account listed in this field is the correct Deposit Error Account that should be used for the selected Deposit Group and Company.
    ​
    ​

  • If the Deposit Error Account is incorrect, note the incorrect account and the correct account.
    ​
    ​

6. Verify the Linked Bank Account Map:

  • While reviewing the Deposit Account Map record, also check the Bank Account field. This field references a record in the Bank Account Maps table.
    ​
    ​

  • Ensure that the Bank Account listed here is the correct destination bank account for the deposits associated with this Deposit Group. While this isn't the direct cause of an incorrect Undeposited Funds or Deposit Error Account, an incorrect Bank Account Map here could lead to other issues.
    ​
    ​

7. Analyze the Incorrect Journal Entry:

  • Review the details of the deposit journal entry that caused the unexpected impact.
    ​
    ​

  • Identify which account (Undeposited Funds or Deposit Error) was incorrectly affected.
    ​
    ​

8. Correct the Deposit Account Map (If Necessary and if you have permissions):

  • If the Undeposited Account in the Deposit Account Map is incorrect, update it to the correct GL account.
    ​
    ​

  • If the Deposit Error Account in the Deposit Account Map is incorrect, update it to the correct GL account.
    ​
    ​

9. Investigate Further if the Issue Persists:

  • If the Deposit Account Maps appear to be configured correctly for the relevant Deposit Group and Company, the issue may stem from an incorrect Deposit Group being selected during the deposit creation process.
    ​
    ​

  • Review the deposit document or transaction to confirm the selected Deposit Group.

10. Contact Support if the Issue Persists:

  • If you have followed the above steps and the issue continues, please contact the support team.
    ​
    ​

  • To help support troubleshoot the issue efficiently, please provide the following information:
    ​
    ​

    • The Deposit Group selected when the deposit was created.
      ​
      ​

    • The Company associated with the deposit.
      ​
      ​

    • The incorrect Undeposited Funds Account that was impacted.
      ​
      ​

    • The correct Undeposited Funds Account that should have been impacted.
      ​
      ​

    • The incorrect Deposit Error Account that was impacted (if applicable).
      ​
      ​

    • The correct Deposit Error Account that should have been impacted (if applicable).
      ​
      ​

    • The Bank Account referenced in the Deposit Account Map.
      ​
      ​

    • Details of the deposit journal entry (journal entry number, date, amounts, accounts involved).
      ​
      ​

    • Screenshots of the relevant Deposit Account Map record.
      ​
      ​

    • A clear description of the steps you have already taken to troubleshoot the issue.

Fields And Definitions

  • Deposit Group: A categorization of payment types that are typically deposited together (e.g., "Daily Cash Receipts," "Weekly Check Deposits"). This field is selected during deposit creation and determines which Deposit Account Map record is used.
    ​
    ​

  • Bank Account: This field references a specific Bank Map record from the Bank Account Maps table. It indicates the destination bank account for the deposited funds.
    ​
    ​

  • Undeposited Account: The General Ledger account used as the initial holding place for customer payments before they are deposited into a bank account. This is the "source" account when creating a deposit journal entry.
    ​
    ​

  • Deposit Error Account: A General Ledger account used to record any discrepancies, overages, shortages, or partial deposits that may occur during the deposit process.
    ​
    ​

  • Transaction Source: For Deposit Account Maps, this field will always be "Deposits," indicating the type of transaction these maps govern.
    ​
    ​

  • Company: The specific company or legal entity within the system to which this Deposit Account Map applies.
    ​
    ​

  • Payment Type: (While mentioned as a determining factor, it's not a direct field on the map itself as described. The combination of Company and Deposit Group typically distinguishes the appropriate map.) The method by which the customer payment was made (e.g., Cash, Check, Credit Card).

Best Practices

  • Establish clear and logical Deposit Groups that align with your deposit processes.
    ​
    ​

  • Carefully review and verify the Undeposited Account and Deposit Error Account configurations for each Deposit Group and Company combination.
    ​
    ​

  • Ensure users are properly trained on selecting the correct Deposit Group during the deposit creation process.
    ​
    ​

  • Regularly audit Deposit Account Maps to ensure they remain accurate, especially after any changes to your chart of accounts or deposit procedures.

Distributor steps in Encompass for fixing a journal entry that hit the wrong bank account by checking the GL account on Bank Account Maps and the Bank Map on Deposit Account Maps. Requires v25.04+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.04

Pre-Conditions

  • You have identified a journal entry that has affected an incorrect bank account balance.
    ​
    ​

  • You have access to the system's Bank Account Maps and Deposit Account Maps tables.
    ​
    ​

  • You have the necessary permissions to view and potentially edit these tables.

Steps

  1. Navigate to the Bank Account Maps Table:

    • Use the universal search bar
      ​
      ​

    • Search for "Bank Account Maps" and select the corresponding table.
      ​
      ​

  2. Locate the Bank Account Map Associated with the Incorrectly Impacted Bank Account:

    • Identify the Bank Map that corresponds to the bank account that was unexpectedly affected by the journal entry.
      ​
      ​

  3. Verify the Linked General Ledger (GL) Account:

    • Once the Bank Account Map is located, examine the Account (GL account) field.
      ​
      ​

    • Ensure that the GL account listed in this field is the correct GL account that should be associated with this bank account.
      ​
      ​

    • If the GL account is incorrect, then make the necessary corrections.
      ​
      ​

  4. Navigate to the Deposit Account Maps Table:

    • Use the universal search functionality within the system.
      ​
      ​

    • Search for "Deposit Account Maps" and select the corresponding table.
      ​
      ​

  5. Locate the Relevant Deposit Account Map Record(s):

    • Identify the Deposit Account Map record(s) that should be using the Bank Account Map identified in Step 2.
      ​
      ​

  6. Confirm the Referenced Bank Map:

    • Within the relevant Deposit Account Map record(s), verify that the Bank Map field is referencing the correct Bank Account Map identified in Step 2.
      ​
      ​

    • If the Bank Map referenced is incorrect, then make the necessary corrections.
      ​
      ​

  7. Contact Support if the Issue Persists:

    • If you have followed the above steps and the issue continues, please contact the support team.
      ​
      ​

    • To help support troubleshoot the issue efficiently, please provide the following information:
      ​
      ​

      • Bank Map (name) of the affected bank account.
        ​
        ​

      • The incorrect bank account that was impacted by the journal entry.
        ​
        ​

      • The correct bank account that should have been impacted.
        ​
        ​

      • Details of the journal entry (journal entry number, date, amounts, accounts involved).
        ​
        ​

      • The GL account currently linked to the Bank Account Map.
        ​
        ​

      • The Bank Map referenced on the relevant Deposit Account Map(s).
        ​
        ​

      • Any screenshots of the Bank Account Maps and Deposit Account Maps configurations.
        ​
        ​

      • A clear description of the steps you have already taken to troubleshoot the issue.

Fields And Definitions

  • Bank Map (name): A unique identifier or name assigned to a Bank Account Map record. This often corresponds to the name of the bank or a specific bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • Company: The specific company or legal entity within the system to which this Bank Account Map applies.
    ​
    ​

  • Account (GL account): The General Ledger account that is directly linked to the bank account defined in this map. Financial transactions related to this bank account will typically impact this GL account.
    ​
    ​

  • Bank Rec Error Account (Optional): A specific GL account used to record errors or discrepancies identified during the bank reconciliation process for this bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • Check Template (Optional): The template used for printing checks associated with this bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • Routing Number (Optional): The bank routing number associated with the bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • Bank Account Number (Optional): The specific account number assigned by the bank.
    ​
    ​

  • Bank Customer Num (Optional): The customer number assigned by the bank for this account.
    ​
    ​

  • Deposit Account Maps: A separate table in the system that links various deposit-related accounts (e.g., undeposited funds, deposit error) to specific Bank Account Maps. This ensures deposits are correctly recorded and reconciled.

Best Practices

  • When closing a bank account, set the associated GL account in the Bank Account Map to Inactive rather than deleting the map. This retains the historical link for accurate bank reconciliations and reporting.
    ​
    ​

  • Establish a clear naming convention for Bank Account Maps to easily identify the associated bank.
    ​
    ​

  • Regularly review Bank Account Maps and Deposit Account Maps to ensure accuracy, especially after any chart of accounts or bank account changes.
    ​
    ​

  • Implement controls to prevent unauthorized modifications to Bank Account Maps and Deposit Account Maps.

Distributor steps for creating Public Dashboards visible before login: build and release a dashboard, set its Sequence (lowest = default landing page) and add the Guest role in Dashboard Roles. Requires v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Steps

A Public Dashboard in Encompass is a standard dashboard that has been specifically configured to be visible on the main Encompass site before a user logs in. This is achieved by granting access to the dashboard to the special 'Guest' user role. While built using the same tools and widgets as internal dashboards, their content is accessible without authentication. The public dashboard with the lowest assigned sequence number determines the default page users first see when navigating to your base Encompass URL.

A. Creating the Dashboard:

  • Click the three dots icon (...) located in the top-left corner of the Encompass screen, above the main menu.
    ​
    ​

  • Select 'New Dashboard' from the options.
    ​
    ​

  • Enter a relevant 'Dashboard Name' and fill in any other necessary information on the form.
    ​
    ​

  • Click 'Save' or 'Save and Close'.
    ​
    ​

  • The system will display the new, blank dashboard. Add and arrange the desired Widgets (tables, charts, reports, etc.) to build the dashboard layout.
    ​
    ​

  • Once the layout is configured, click the 'Save' icon on the dashboard.
    ​
    ​

  • To make the dashboard accessible, click 'Save as released'. (You can use 'Save as Draft' if you are still designing the dashboard and it's not ready for general use).
    ​
    ​
    ​

B. Setting the Sequence:

  • Navigate to the Dashboards table (you can use the Universal Search).
    ​
    ​

  • Find the dashboard record you just created or wish to make public.
    ​
    ​

  • Edit the dashboard record.
    ​
    ​

  • Locate the Sequence field and enter a numerical value.
    ​
    ​

  • This number controls the order in which dashboards appear in the left-hand menu for logged-in users.
    ​
    ​

  • Crucially, for public dashboards, the one with the lowest sequence number will be the default page displayed when navigating to your Encompass site before logging in.
    ​
    ​

  • Save the changes to the dashboard record.
    ​
    ​
    ​

C. Making the Dashboard Public (Sharing with Guest Role):

  • While viewing the desired dashboard record in the Dashboards table (or after finding it again), click the 'Sub-Tables' button (or related items menu).
    ​
    ​

  • Select 'Dashboard Roles' from the list.
    ​
    ​

  • Click the 'Add Dashboard Role' button (or similar action like 'New' or '+').
    ​
    ​

  • In the form for the new Dashboard Role, select the Guest role from the Role dropdown list.
    ​
    ​

  • Save the Dashboard Role record.
    ​
    ​

  • Adding the 'Guest' role makes the dashboard 'public', meaning it will be visible on the main Encompass page before a user logs in.

Fields And Definitions

  • Dashboard Name: (On Dashboards Table) The title of the dashboard as it appears in the menu and at the top of the dashboard page.
    ​
    ​

  • Sequence: (On Dashboards Table) A numerical field that determines the display order in the left-hand menu. For dashboards shared with the 'Guest' role, the dashboard with the lowest sequence number becomes the default landing page before login.
    ​
    ​

  • Role: (In Dashboard Roles Sub-Table) Specifies which user role has access to the dashboard. Assigning the Guest role makes the dashboard public.
    ​
    ​

  • Description: (On Dashboards Table) A field to provide a concise summary of the dashboard's purpose or content.
    ​
    ​

  • Keywords: (On Dashboards Table) A field where you can enter a comma-separated list of relevant words or phrases related to the dashboard's content.

Best Practices

  • Sequence Planning: Carefully consider the sequence numbers assigned to public dashboards. The public dashboard with the lowest sequence number will be the very first page users see when accessing your main Encompass URL (e.g., https://yourcompany.encompass.com/).
    ​
    ​

  • Login Behavior: While public dashboards are visible before login, accessing any non-public dashboard or system area via a direct link (e.g., https://yourcompany.encompass8.com/Home?DashboardID=100100&TableName=Products) will automatically redirect the user to the login page first. After successful login, they will be taken to their intended destination.
    ​
    ​

  • Mandatory Login Dashboard: Every Encompass system includes a default 'Login' dashboard which contains the login widget. This dashboard is always public (shared with 'Guest') and cannot be removed or made non-public. Ensure its sequence number is considered relative to any other public dashboards you create if you don't want it to be the very first page loaded. Typically, it's given a higher sequence number than the desired initial landing page.
    ​
    ​

  • Content Sensitivity: Be mindful that any data displayed on a public dashboard is visible to anyone who accesses your Encompass URL, without needing to log in. Do not display sensitive or confidential information on public dashboards.
    ​
    ​

  • Optimize for Search Engines: If you want your public dashboards to be easily found via external search engines (like Google), make effective use of the Description and Keywords fields on the Dashboard record. Write clear, concise descriptions and include relevant keywords that accurately reflect the dashboard's content.

Creating Bin Count Tasks

16989990:
Distributor guide to troubleshoot a wrong price or missing promotion on an invoice in Encompass: check the price calculator, qualifying units, promotion eligibility and the invoice audit. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Steps

1. Confirm Product and Expected Price: Identify the specific product on the invoice that has the incorrect price. Determine the correct expected price for this product based on the promotion you believe should be applied.
​
2. Investigate Price Calculation:

  • Click on the price calculator within the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Compare the applied promotion with the promotion you expect to be applied.
    ​
    ​

-If the customer should be qualified for the promotion:

  • Check if the invoice price was manually overridden.
    ​
    ​

  • Verify if the applied promotion results in a lower price than the expected promotion.

-If the customer should NOT be qualified for the promotion:

  • Investigate the reason why the system did not qualify the customer for the expected promotion (refer to step 4).

3. Verify Qualifying Units:

  • Confirm the total number of units for the product on the invoice that should qualify for the promotion. This includes the shipped quantity plus any backordered quantity at the time the pricing was calculated.
    ​
    ​

  • You may need to consult the customer's order history to determine the backordered quantity at the time the invoice pricing was initially calculated. This is crucial as backorders can influence promotion eligibility based on minimum unit requirements.

4. Confirm Customer Promotion Eligibility:
​
-Verify if the customer meets the criteria for the promotion:

  • Location-based: Ensure the customer's location is within a region or market associated with the promotion (check promotion locations or market).
    ​
    ​

  • Customer-specific: Confirm the customer is linked to the promotion through a designated customer promotion zone, market or a specific promotion customer assignment.

5. Review Invoice Audit:

  • Click the Invoice Audit button on the Invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Click the "Diff" link on any of the records to identify when the pricing for the product changed or when the product was added to the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Click on the "Trans audit" link to the right of the specific product line item, on the Diff screen, to view a complete history of transactions related to that product on the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Analyze the audit trail to determine if the promotion was manually overridden by a user or if it was automatically calculated by the system.

6. Examine Subtables and Transaction Audit Details:

  • Within the invoice audit, select "Subtables" and then "Transaction Audit" to see the detailed transactions for each step of the invoice creation and modification process.
    ​
    ​

  • Review this information to understand the origin of the data, such as what was initially imported from a handheld device, what changes were manually applied (overrides), etc. This can help identify if pricing discrepancies originated from external systems or manual adjustments.

Fields And Definitions

  • Invoice ID: A unique identifier for the specific sales invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Product ID: A unique identifier for the specific product on the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Expected Promotion: The name or code of the promotion that should have been applied to the product.
    ​
    ​

  • Actual Promotion Applied: The name or code of the promotion that was actually applied to the product on the invoice (if any).
    ​
    ​

  • Promotion Locations: The geographical regions or markets set on a Promotion.
    ​
    ​

  • Customer Promotion Zone: A grouping of customers that are eligible for specific promotions.
    ​
    ​

  • Promotion Customer: A specific customer who is directly assigned to a particular promotion.
    ​
    ​

  • Invoice Audit: A log that tracks all changes and transactions related to an invoice, including pricing modifications, product additions, and user actions.
    ​
    ​

  • Diff Screen (Invoice Audit): A view within the invoice audit that highlights the differences between versions of the invoice, showing what data was added, modified, or deleted.
    ​
    ​

  • Transaction Audit (Invoice/Product Level): A detailed history of all transactions and changes related to the entire invoice or a specific product line item on the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Customer History.Last Price: A field in the customer's historical data that records the last price paid by the customer for a specific product.
    ​
    ​

  • Mobile User Sync: The process by which data on a mobile device is synced with the server.

Best Practices

  • Ensure customer promotion data (location, promotion zone, customer promotion assignments) is accurate and up-to-date.
    ​
    ​

  • Regularly review promotion configurations and ensure they are correctly set up with the appropriate locations, customer segments, and qualifying criteria.
    ​
    ​

  • Train mobile users on the importance of syncing their devices regularly to ensure they have the latest pricing and promotion data.
    ​
    ​

  • Implement controls and audit processes for manual price overrides on invoices.
    ​
    ​

  • When processing returns, always verify the "customer history.last price" field, especially for products with no prior return history, as it will reflect current pricing.
16989991:
What to do when a Fintech payment hit the bank but invoices still show open in Encompass: check 820 Remittance exchange tasks, ask Fintech to resend, or clear balances with credit invoices on a load sheet.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You know the invoices were paid through Fintech.
    ​
    ​

  • You've confirmed the Fintech payment hit the bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • The invoices in Encompass still show an open balance.

Steps

  1. Check Encompass Exchange Tasks:
    ​
    ​

    • Go to the "Exchange Tasks" table
      ​
      ​

    • Look for any tasks related to the "820 Remittance" and your specific Fintech Configuration(s). You might need to filter or search for these.
      ​
      ​

    • Check the status of these tasks. Look for any that are in a "Warning" or "Error" status.
      ​
      ​

    • If you find any warning or error messages, carefully read the details.
      ​
      ​

    • Attempt to address the warnings or errors based on the information provided. This might involve re-running a task, correcting a configuration setting, or investigating a data issue. Consult Encompass documentation or internal procedures if you're unsure how to resolve the specific warning or error.
      ​
      ​

    • After addressing any warnings or errors, monitor Encompass to see if the payment status of the affected invoices updates.
      ​
      ​

    • If the exchange tasks are running without errors or if addressing the errors doesn't resolve the issue, proceed to the next step.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  2. Try Fintech First (If Exchange Tasks are clear):
    ​
    ​

    • Contact Fintech support and tell them about the problem.
      ​
      ​

    • Ask them to resend the 820 Remittance file just for those invoices.
      ​
      ​

    • Ask them when they expect to resend the file.
      ​
      ​

    • Give Fintech the invoice numbers and proof that we got the payment.
      ​
      ​

    • Keep an eye on Encompass to see if the payment status changes after Fintech says they've resent the file.
      ​
      ​

    • If it's taking too long or Fintech can't resend it, go to the next steps.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  3. Fix it with Credit Invoices in Encompass (If Fintech can't help quickly):
    ​
    ​

    • Create a new Loadsheet in Encompass. Make sure it starts in a "New" status.
      ​
      ​

    • Click "Add Invoice" in the new loadsheet.
      ​
      ​

    • Create a new invoice for the customer who has the unpaid invoice.
      ​
      ​

    • In this new invoice, put in the amount you received from Fintech in the received field. (Please note if you are receiving money from a third party, this should be a positive amount. If you are paying a third party, this should be a negative.)
      ​
      ​

    • For "Payment Type," pick the same Accounts Receivable (AR) account we use for Fintech payments.
      ​
      ​

    • Save the invoice.
      ​
      ​

    • Do this for each invoice that's showing as unpaid.
      ​
      ​

    • Go back into the credit invoice you just made.
      ​
      ​

    • Click the "Apply Payment" button.
      ​
      ​

    • On the right side of the screen, find and click on the original, unpaid invoice.
      ​
      ​

    • Save. This will make the balance on the original invoice zero.
      ​
      ​

    • Do this for all the credit invoices and their matching unpaid invoices.
      ​
      ​

    • Once you've done this for all the invoices, Load the Load Sheet.
      ​
      ​

    • Return and Balance the loadsheet to make sure everything is correct.
      ​
      ​

    • Apply this loadsheet to the bank deposit where the Fintech payment went.
      ​
      ​

    • Note: If that bank deposit is already finalized, create a new deposit and make a note of which deposit the payment should have been linked to for your records.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  4. If it's still not fixed, contact Encompass Support and give them this information:
    ​
    ​

    • Verification that the Fintech payment was received and the date.
      ​
      ​

    • The numbers of the invoices that are wrong.
      ​
      ​

    • If you tried contacting Fintech and what happened.
      ​
      ​

    • Any steps taken to attempt to correct the data manaully
      ​
      ​

    • Any error messages or anything unexpected you saw in Encompass.

Fields And Definitions

  • Fintech: The outside company we use to process payments.
    ​
    ​

  • 820 Remittance File: An electronic file Fintech sends us that says which invoices they paid.
    ​
    ​

  • Exchange Task: An automatic process in Encompass that talks to outside systems like Fintech.
    ​
    ​

  • Exchange Configurations: The settings in Encompass that tell it how to talk to outside systems/
    ​
    ​

  • Credit Invoice: An invoice that lowers or cancels out the amount owed on an old invoice. Here, we use it to fix the wrong balance.
    ​
    ​

  • Off-day: Making a loadsheet when we don't usually process them.
    ​
    ​

  • Deposit: A record in Encompass of money going into our bank account.
    ​
    ​

  • AR Account (Accounts Receivable): The accounting record of money that customers owe us.
    ​
    ​

  • Warning Status (Exchange Task): Indicates a potential issue with the data exchange that might need attention.
    ​
    ​

  • Error Status (Exchange Task): Indicates a failure in the data exchange process that needs to be resolved.

Best Practices

  • Regularly check the Encompass Exchange Tasks for any warnings or errors related to Fintech integrations.
    ​
    ​

  • Always check Encompass to make sure payments went through after Fintech confirms.
    ​
    ​

  • Keep good records of Fintech payment reports and the Encompass invoices they match.
    ​
    ​

  • If something doesn't look right, try checking Exchange Tasks first, then try to fix it with Fintech.
    ​
    ​

  • When you make credit invoices, double-check the customer, invoice numbers, and amounts to avoid mistakes.
    ​
    ​

  • Write down all the steps you take when troubleshooting in case we need to look into it more later.

16989994:
Distributor guide for when a rep's sales, inventory or backorder data doesn't show on the Encompass Mobile handheld: read Customer History date arrays, check store depletions, then manually sync. v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • Permission to run Scheduled Tasks - Global Setting Edit

Steps

1. Identify Customer and Product: Determine the specific customer account that was involved in the sales activity. Identify the specific product that the sales representative interacted with. 2. Identify Date and Expected Data: Confirm the exact date when the sales representative performed the action. Understand what data the user expects to see on the handheld device as a result of this action (e.g., updated inventory levels, a new order, a change in status). 3. Access Customer History Table: Navigate to the Customer History table. Apply filters to isolate the records specifically for the identified custome and the relevant product. 4. Examine Date and Data Arrays: Locate the "Date Array" field for the filtered records. This field contains a comma-separated list of date ranges. Compare the "Date Array" with the "Inventory Array," "Num Units Array," and "Backorder Array." Understanding the Arrays: The position of a value in the "Inventory Array," "Num Units Array" and "Backorder Array" corresponds to the date range at the same position in the "Date Array" For example, if the "Date Array" is "1/1/2025, 1/31/2025, 2/1/2025" and the "Units Array" is " , 2," this indicates: - No units were purchased during the date range starting on "1/1/2025" and ending before "1/31/2025". - 2 units were purchased on "1/31/2025". - No units were purchased during the date range starting on "2/1/2025". 5. Analyze Missing Data:- Is data missing in the Customer History table? If No: The data appears to be present in the customer history. Instruct the mobile user to manually sync their handheld device using the sync button on the home screen. After sycncing, ask them to confirm if the expected data is now visible. If Yes: Identify the specific missing data. Is it related to inventory levels, units purchased, or backorders? Check Store Depletions (if retailer inventory related): If the missing data pertains to inventory, investigate the Store Depletions records for the relevant date to confirm if inventory was properly accounted for on the expected day.

Fields And Definitions

  • Date Array: A field in the Customer History table containing a comma-separated list of date ranges representing periods of activity or data changes.
    ​
    ​

  • Inventory Array: A field in the Customer History table containing comma-separated values representing the inventory levels corresponding to the date ranges in the "Date Array."
    ​
    ​

  • Num Units Array: A field in the Customer History table containing comma-separated values representing the number of units purchased corresponding to the date ranges in the "Date Array.
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder Array: A field in the Customer History table containing comma-separated values representing the number of units on backorder corresponding to the date ranges in the "Date Array."
    ​
    ​

  • Store Depletions: Records detailing the reduction of inventory within a specific store or location.
    ​
    ​

  • Rebuild Customer History Date Array: A Scheduled Task that specifically rebuilds the date and associated data arrays in the Customer History table.
    ​
    ​Important: This script rebuilds only the date-related arrays and preserves manually set statuses.
    ​
    ​

  • Rebuild_Customer_History: A database script that completely resets the customer history, including any manually set statuses.
    ​
    ​Caution: Avoid using this script unless explicitly instructed by support, as it can lead to data loss and takes a significant amount of time to run.

Best Practices

  • Ensure sales reps manually sync their handheld devices regularly, especially after any sales activities or account updates.
    ​
    ​

  • Verify data accuracy on the server before assuming an issue with the handheld sync.

  • Exercise caution when running Scheduled Tasks. Always understand the potential impact before execution.
16989995:
Distributor overview of Comparison Report types in Encompass (products, customers, purchases, pricing, AR, surveys, ranking, compound, discount) with a video. Requires v24.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 24.01

Watch video on YouTube

Steps

Types of Comparison Reports:
​
​

  • Products: Allows you to analyze your product data by organizing it into parent-child relationships and displaying product counts. You can filter based on product attributes like brand and see how different product categories are distributed across other characteristics like inventory status and much more.
    ​
    ​

  • Customers: Similar to the Products report, this focuses on your customer data. It enables you to group customers by different attributes like assigned sales representative and view metrics such as the number of customers in each group, with the ability to filter based on customer characteristics.
    ​
    ​

  • Purchases: This report mirrors the Sales Comparison Report structure but focuses on your purchasing data. You can analyze vendor performance, track the quantity of goods purchased over time, or compare purchase patterns across different dimensions like vendor and month.
    ​
    ​

  • Pricing: This report displays all available pricing data for your products based on a selected effective date and customer. It allows you to see list prices, discounts, and calculated unit prices but reflects the basic pricing setup in the system.
    ​
    ​

  • InvoicePricing: This report simulates the pricing logic used when creating an actual invoice. It considers complex pricing structures and promotions, showing the final price a customer would likely pay, and can be influenced by factors like minimum purchase quantities.
    ​
    ​

  • AccountsReceivable: This report focuses on AR Account data such as overdue invoices or AR aging. It offers a wider range of value options compared to other comparison reports and includes specific filters for statement dates and overdue accounts.
    ​
    ​

  • Surveys: This unique report type allows you to analyze survey results. Survey questions become the values displayed, and you can group responses by attributes like who the survey was assigned to and the completion date, showing individual answers and customers who haven't responded.

16989996:
Explains what Case Equivalents (Case Equivs, CEs) are in Encompass and how they're calculated from product volume per case and the Case Equivs table, so volumes can be compared across package sizes. v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

What are Case Equivalents?
​
​

  • Case Equivalents (often abbreviated as "Case Equiv" or "CE") are a standardized unit of volume used in various industries, particularly those dealing with the sale and distribution of goods that come in different sizes and packaging. Instead of simply counting the number of physical cases, case equivalents provide a common metric to measure and compare the total volume of products sold, shipped, or inventoried.
    ​
    ​

  • Think of it as a way to "normalize" different product sizes into a standard "case" unit for easier analysis and reporting.

Why Use Case Equivalents?

Using case equivalents offers several benefits:
​
​

  • Standardized Measurement: It allows for the comparison of sales or volumes across products that come in different case sizes or configurations. For example, comparing the volume of sales of a product sold in cases of 12 units to another sold in cases of 24 units becomes straightforward.
    ​
    ​

  • Accurate Volume Tracking: It provides a more accurate representation of the total volume being moved or sold, which is crucial for logistics, warehousing, and supply chain management.
    ​
    ​

  • Consistent Reporting: It enables consistent reporting across different product lines and sales channels, providing a unified view of overall business activity.
    ​
    ​

  • Pricing and Promotions: It can be used as a basis for pricing strategies, promotional offers (e.g., discounts based on equivalent case volume), and sales targets.
    ​
    ​

  • Inventory Management: It helps in managing inventory levels by providing a consistent unit for tracking overall product volume, regardless of the actual packaging.

Steps

"Case Equivalents" (Case Equivs) represent the volume of a product, not necessarily a direct one-to-one count of the physical cases. The system uses a defined standard volume for a "case equivalent" of a specific product or product category and then converts the actual volume sold (based on the number of physical cases and the volume per case) into this standardized unit.

Calculation Steps:
​
​

  • Define Standard Case Equivalent Volume: For each product or potentially product category within Encompass, a standard volume is defined as equal to one case equivalent. This volume could be in units (e.g., 24 items), weight (e.g., in pounds or kilograms), or fluid ounces/milliliters. Standard volume calculations for case equivs live on the case equivs table where you can define a case equiv type and the amount of volume for a standard 'case'.
    ​
    ​

  • Define Volume per Physical Case: For each product, Encompass stores the volume contained in one physical case. This could be the number of units per case multiplied by the volume per unit, or a total volume for the entire case. This is set based on the package of the product.
    ​
    ​

  • Calculate Total Volume Sold: When a sale occurs, the number of physical cases sold is multiplied by the volume per physical case to determine the total volume of that product sold.

Total Volume = Number of Physical Cases Sold × Volume per Physical Case

  • Example: 2 cases × 152.163102 ounces/case = 304.326204 ounces

​
Convert Total Volume to Case Equivalents: The total volume sold is then divided by the defined standard case equivalent volume for that product (or product category) to arrive at the Case Equiv value.

  • Case Equivalents = Total Volume Sold / Standard Case Equivalent Volume
    ​
    ​

  • In the example: 304.326204 ounces / 304.3260 ounces/case equiv ≈ 1 case equiv
    ​
    ​

  • Therefore, the Case Equivalent value reflects how many "standard volume units" were sold, even if the product was packaged and sold in a different physical case size.

Fields And Definitions

  • Case Equivalent (Case Equiv): A standardized unit representing the volume of a product, used for consistent reporting and comparison across different packaging sizes. It may not always equal one physical case.
    ​
    ​

  • Comparison Report View: A report that allows for the comparison of data, potentially showing both the number of physical cases and the calculated Case Equivalent value.
    ​
    ​

  • 'Case Equivs' Table: A table within the system defines the standard volume or calculation rules for Case Equivalents for different products.

Best Practices

  • Understand that 'Case Equivalent' is a measure of volume and not necessarily a direct count of physical cases.
    ​
    ​

  • Familiarize yourself with the location of any 'Case Equivs' tables or definitions within the system if you have access.
    ​
    ​

  • When inquiring about Case Equivalents, always specify the Product ID you are asking about, as the definition can be product-specific.
16989997:
Distributor guide to troubleshoot backorders on an invoice in Encompass: check Invoice Transactions, Customer History backorder arrays, backfills and reason codes with Autobackorder. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You have access to the relevant database or system containing invoice and customer history information.
    ​
    ​

  • You have the invoice number of the impacted invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • You have identified a specific product on the invoice that is experiencing a backorder issue.

Steps

1. Navigate to the Invoices table and select the invoice.2. Click the Data tab at the top.3. Click Subtables -> Invoice Transactions4. Take note of the key Invoice Transaction Fields for the backordered Product:Num units: The quantity of the product that was delivered on this invoice.Backorder: The quantity of the product that was backordered on this specific invoice line item.Ordered: The total quantity of the product that was ordered at the time the truck was loaded (this is equal to Num units + the total backorder at that time).5. Navigate to Customer History table using the Universal Search bar.6. Filter to the Customer and Product you are investigating.7. Review Customer History Fields:Date array: This field contains a history of dates related to backorder events for this product and customer.Backorder array: This field contains a history of backorder quantities associated with the dates in the date array.Backorder: The current total backordered quantity for this product for this customer.Backfill: The quantity of the product that has been backfilled (shipped to fulfill a previous backorder).Backorder date: The date the most recent backorder was placed or updated.8. Investigate Reason Codes on the impacted invoice:Note the Reason Code associated with the backordered Product.9. Navigate to the Reasons table. 10. Filter to the noted Reason code.11. Check the value of the Autobackorder field. A value of True indicates the system automatically backordered the item based on the Reason code.

Fields And Definitions

  • Num Units (Invoice Transactions) - The quantity of a specific product that was delivered to the customer on the particular invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder (Invoice Transactions) - The quantity of a specific product that was not delivered on the invoice and was marked as backordered (on that specific invoice line item).
    ​
    ​

  • Ordered (Invoice Transactions) - The total quantity of a specific product that the customer ordered on the invoice line item at the time the order was processed for shipment. Calculated as Num units + Total backorder at that time.
    ​
    ​

  • Date Array (Customer History) -History of dates associated with backorder events for a specific product and customer.
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder Array (Customer History) - Backorder quantities for the dates recorded in the Date array for a specific product and customer.
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder (Customer History) - The current total quantity of a specific product that is backordered for a particular customer across all open backorders. This is often calculated by summing the 'Backorder' field from relevant invoice transactions.
    ​
    ​

  • Backfill (Customer History) - The total quantity of a specific product that has been shipped to the customer to fulfill previous backorders.
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder Date (Customer History) - The date when the most recent backorder was placed or when an existing backorder's date was updated (e.g., when a new invoice with a backorder for the same product was created).
    ​
    ​

  • Reason Code (Invoice Transactions) - A code assigned to a product line item on the invoice that explains why a certain action (like a backorder) occurred.
    ​
    ​

  • Autobackorder (Reasons Table) - A field in the reasons table (associated with reason codes) that indicates whether the system automatically initiates a backorder based on that specific reason code (true or false).
    ​
    ​

  • Out of stock flag - An indicator that appears when the ordered quantity on an invoice transaction is greater than the number of units delivered (invoicetrans.ordered > Invoicetrans.num units).
    ​
    ​

  • Backorder expired - An indicator that appears when the number of units delivered on an invoice transaction is zero, and the backordered quantity on that transaction is less than zero (invoicetrans.num units = 0 and invoicetrans.backorder < 0). This likely indicates a backorder that was not fulfilled and potentially canceled or expired.
    ​
    ​

  • Backfilled - An indicator that appears when the number of units delivered on an invoice transaction is greater than zero, and the backordered quantity on that transaction is less than zero (invoicetrans.num units > 0 and invoicetrans.backorder < 0). This suggests that some of the backordered quantity was subsequently fulfilled on the same invoice or a later shipment.

Best Practices

  • Focus on One Product at a Time: When troubleshooting, isolate the issue by focusing on a single problematic product on the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • Document Your Findings: Keep a record of the values you observe in each field during your troubleshooting process.
    ​
    ​

  • Understand the Data Relationships: Recognize that invoice transaction data provides a snapshot of the order at the time of invoicing, while the customer history table maintains a running total of backorders for a customer and product.
    ​
    ​

  • Consider the Timing of End-of-Day Processes: Remember that backorders on the customer history table do not expire until the end-of-day process is run for the backorder expiration date.

16990000:
Guide to creating a custom API Command in Encompass: define its purpose, set up API tokens and permission codes, build and test the logic, and fix errors like 401 Unauthorized. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You have access to the API management interface of your system.
    ​
    ​

  • You have the necessary permissions to create new API commands.
    ​
    ​

  • You understand the purpose and functionality of the API command you intend to create.
    ​
    ​

  • You have a clear understanding of the data source (if applicable) and the desired outcome of the API command.
    ​
    ​

  • You may need specific API tokens or credentials depending on the API command's function.
    ​
    ​

  • It is recommended to have a test environment to build and test your API command before deploying it to your live environment.

Steps

  1. Define the API Command's Purpose:
    ​
    ​

    • Clearly define what this new API command should accomplish. What data should it retrieve, process, or modify? What will be the input and output?
      ​
      ​

    • Example: Generating a document from data, importing data into a table.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  2. Identify Necessary Resources and Functionality:
    ​
    ​

    • Determine what components or features your API command will need to interact with. This might include:
      ​
      ​

      • Specific data sources (e.g., other APIs, databases, documents).
        ​
        ​

      • Existing API functionalities that can be leveraged.
        ​
        ​

      • Custom code or logic (e.g., cloud functions).
        ​
        ​

      • Specific permissions required to access data or perform actions.
        ​
        ​

    • Example: Needing to inherit TableImport functionality for importing data.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  3. Create the API Command:
    ​
    ​

    • Use the API management interface to create a new API command.
      ​
      ​

    • Provide a clear and descriptive name and any necessary identifiers for your API command (e.g., API Command ID).
      ​
      ​

    • Configure the API command based on its intended purpose. This may involve:
      ​
      ​

      • Defining parameters that the API command will accept as input.
        ​
        ​

      • Specifying the logic or code that will be executed when the API command is called.
        ​
        ​

      • Setting up connections to data sources or other APIs.
        ​
        ​
        ​

  4. Configure Authentication and Authorization:
    ​
    ​

    • Determine how the API command will be authenticated and authorized. This often involves using API tokens.
      ​
      ​

    • API Tokens:
      ​
      ​

      • If your API command needs to access protected resources or perform specific actions, you will likely need an API token with the appropriate permissions.
        ​
        ​

      • Create a new API token or use an existing one.
        ​
        ​

      • Permissions: Ensure the API token has all the necessary permissions required for the API command to function correctly. This might include permissions to view, create, edit, or delete specific data or resources. You may need to consult documentation or support to identify the required permission codes. You can also (optionally) set the 'Required Permission' value on the API Command record itself. This will cause the system to always validate that the user or token calling the API has that specific permission.
        ​
        ​

      • Example: Needing "DocumentView", "EDI view", and potentially "ReportView" permissions. The Permission Code Arr field in the API Token settings is where these can be added, separated by '!'.
        ​
        ​
        ​

  5. Implement the API Command's Logic:
    ​
    ​

    • Implement the core functionality of your API command. This may involve writing code (e.g., in a cloud function) to:
      ​
      ​

      • Retrieve data from specified sources.
        ​
        ​

      • Process or transform data as needed.
        ​
        ​

      • Interact with other APIs or system components.
        ​
        ​

      • Format the output of the API command.
        ​
        ​
        ​

  6. Testing the API Command:
    ​
    ​

    • Thoroughly test the new API command in a test environment.
      ​
      ​

    • Send various requests with different parameters to ensure it functions as expected under different conditions.
      ​
      ​

    • Verify that the output is correct and that any intended actions are performed successfully.
      ​
      ​

    • Check for any errors or unexpected behavior.
      ​
      ​

    • Example: Encountering a 401 Unauthorized error or an empty response during testing.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  7. Deployment (Optional):
    ​
    ​

    • Once you have thoroughly tested the API command and are confident in its functionality, you can deploy it to your production environment if necessary. Follow your system's deployment procedures.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  8. Documentation:
    ​
    ​

    • Document the purpose, functionality, input parameters, output format, and any specific requirements or considerations for your new API command. This will be helpful for yourself and other users who may need to interact with it.
      ​
      ​
      ​

If you encounter issues:
​

  • Review Error Messages: Carefully examine any error messages you receive for clues about the problem.
    ​
    ​

  • Check API Token Permissions: Ensure the API token you are using has all the necessary permissions. Insufficient permissions are a common cause of errors (e.g., 401 Unauthorized, permission denied).
    ​
    ​

  • Verify API Command Logic: Double-check the code or configuration of your API command for any errors or incorrect settings.
    ​
    ​

  • Consult Documentation: Refer to your system's API documentation for information on specific methods, data types, and required permissions.
    ​
    ​

  • Contact Support: If you are unable to resolve the issue, reach out to your system's support team for assistance.
    ​
    ​

  • Provide the following information to support:
    ​
    ​

    • API Command ID of the new API command.
      ​
      ​

    • Detailed description of the issue and the steps you took to reproduce it.
      ​
      ​

    • Any error messages you are receiving.
      ​
      ​

    • Information about the API token you are using and its permissions.
      ​
      ​

    • Any relevant code snippets or configurations.

Fields And Definitions

  • API Command: A defined set of instructions that enables interaction between software systems.
    ​
    ​

  • API Token: A security key that verifies the identity of an application or user making an API request and grants access based on associated permissions.
    ​
    ​

  • Authentication: The process of verifying the identity of the user or application accessing the API.
    ​
    ​

  • Authorization: The process of determining what actions or resources the authenticated user or application is allowed to access.
    ​
    ​

  • Parameter: An input value that can be passed to an API command to customize its behavior.
    ​
    ​

  • Cloud Function: A serverless piece of code that can be executed in response to an event or an API call.
    ​

Best Practices

  • Start Simple: Begin with a basic version of your API command and add complexity incrementally, testing at each stage.
    ​
    ​

  • Follow Naming Conventions: Use clear and consistent naming conventions for your API commands and parameters.
    ​
    ​

  • Implement Error Handling: Include error handling in your API command logic to manage potential issues gracefully.
    ​
    ​

  • Secure Your API: Follow security best practices for API development, including proper authentication and authorization.
    ​
    ​

  • Monitor Your API: Once deployed, monitor the performance and usage of your API command.
