  1. Verify File Origin and Modification:

    • Ensure the PO file was downloaded directly from Boston Beer or Heineken.

    • Confirm that the file has not been modified after download. Any modifications, even seemingly minor ones, can cause import errors.
      ​
      ​

  2. Boston Beer File Verification:

    • Location and Supplier Selection: In the Encompass PO Importer, select the appropriate location and "Boston Beer Company" as the supplier.

    • Column Headers: Verify that the Boston Beer file contains the following column headers, exactly as shown:

      • SalesOrder#

      • ShipDate

      • PO

      • BBCSKU

      • Quantity

    • File Format: Ensure the file is in the correct format (XLS or XLSX).

    • Re-upload: Attempt to upload the file again.
      ​
      ​

  3. Heineken File Verification:

    • Location and Supplier Selection: In the Encompass PO Importer, select the appropriate location and "Heineken" as the supplier.

    • Column Headers and Row: Verify that the Heineken file has the correct column headers, and that those headers are located on Row 6.

    • Data Start Row: Ensure that the PO data begins on the row immediately following the header row (Row 7, if headers are on Row 6). Remove any extraneous rows or information above the header row.

    • Required Columns: Verify that the Heineken file contains the following column headers, exactly as shown:

      • RequestedDeliveryDate

      • OrderNo.

      • ItemNo.

      • OrderQuantity

    • File Format: Ensure the file is in the correct format (XLS or XLSX).

    • Re-upload: Attempt to upload the file again.
      ​
      ​

  4. Check for Hidden Characters/Formatting:

    • Open the file in a spreadsheet editor (e.g., Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets).

    • Check for any hidden characters, extra spaces, or unusual formatting in the header row and data rows. These can sometimes be invisible but still cause parsing errors.

    • If possible, try copying the data into a new, clean spreadsheet file.
      ​
      ​

  5. Test with Example File:

    • If available, try importing the Heineken example file that was provided. This will help determine if the issue is with the user's file or the import process itself.
      ​
      ​

  6. If the issue persists:

    • Contact Encompass Technologies Support immediately.

    • Provide the following information to the support team:

      • The exact error message received.

      • The Boston Beer or Heineken PO file that is causing the error.

      • A screenshot of the error message.

      • The steps you have already taken to troubleshoot the issue.

      • The example file you are using.

Fields And Definitions

  • PO: Purchase Order. A commercial document issued by a buyer to a seller, indicating the types, quantities, and agreed prices for products or services.

  • PO Importer: The Encompass system tool used to upload and process PO files.

  • Location: The specific location within the Encompass system where the PO is being imported.

  • Supplier: The company providing the goods or services (e.g., "Boston Beer Company," "Heineken").

  • SalesOrder#: (Boston Beer) The sales order number associated with the purchase.

  • ShipDate: (Boston Beer) The date the order is scheduled to be shipped.

  • BBCSKU: (Boston Beer) Boston Beer Company's Stock Keeping Unit (SKU) number.

  • Quantity: (Boston Beer) The quantity of the product ordered.

  • RequestedDeliveryDate: (Heineken) The date the order is requested to be delivered.

  • OrderNo.: (Heineken) The order number.

  • ItemNo.: (Heineken) The item number.

  • OrderQuantity: (Heineken) The quantity of the product ordered.

  • XLS: A file extension for a spreadsheet file format used by Microsoft Excel (older versions).

  • XLSX: A file extension for a spreadsheet file format used by Microsoft Excel (newer versions).

  • Column Header: The label at the top of a column in a spreadsheet that describes the data in that column.

  • Row: A horizontal series of data in a table or spreadsheet.

Best Practices

  • Download Files Directly: Always download PO files directly from the supplier's official source (e.g., Boston Beer's or Heineken's website or portal).

  • Avoid Manual Modification: Minimize or avoid manual modification of PO files after downloading. If modifications are necessary, be extremely careful to maintain the exact column headers and data formats.

  • Verify File Format: Ensure the PO files are in the expected file format (XLS or XLSX).

  • Check Column Headers: Double-check that the column headers in the PO file exactly match the requirements of the Encompass PO Importer. Pay close attention to spelling, capitalization, and spacing.

  • Remove Extraneous Data: Remove any unnecessary rows, columns, or information from the PO file, especially before the header row.

  • Use a Template (If Available): If Encompass provides a template for PO file imports, use that template to ensure proper formatting.

  • Regularly Check for Updates: Ensure that your Encompass system is up-to-date with the latest patches and updates, as these may include fixes for import issues.

  • Test with Small Files: When troubleshooting, try importing a small PO file with only a few line items to isolate the problem.

  • Document Errors: Keep a record of any errors encountered, including the error message, the file being imported, and the steps taken to troubleshoot. This information will be helpful for support and for future troubleshooting.

16990008:
Distributor troubleshooting for BudNet VIPR pricing exceptions in Encompass: check on/off-premise Customer Promotion Zones and the Legacy Frontline Zone on the Distribution Area. Requires v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You're receiving exceptions in your Value In Price Reporting (VIPR) report from BudNet.
    ​
    ​

  • The exceptions indicate a mismatch between the expected frontline price or discount price from BudNet and the frontline price reported in your Encompass system.
    ​
    ​

  • You have different pricing structures for on-premise and off-premise customers for the same products.
    ​
    ​

  • You have access to your BudNet portal and your Encompass system, specifically Customer Promotion Zones, Distribution Area settings, and potentially Exchange Task files.

Steps

  1. Identify the Specific Exception: Note the Wholesaler ID, Business Date, and Product Description Codes (PDCNs) from the VIPR exception report. The URL provided in the exception can often give you direct access to the file status in BudNet.
    ​
    ​

  2. Review Customer Promotion Zones in Encompass:
    ​
    ​

    • For the customer(s) listed in the exception, navigate to their "Customers Promotion Zones" in Encompass.
      ​
      ​

    • Verify if the customer is assigned to the correct promotion zones based on their on-premise or off-premise status.
      ​
      ​

    • Example Scenario 1 (Incorrect Zone): If an off-premise customer is in an on-premise promotion zone, they might be receiving the on-premise price when BudNet expects the off-premise price.
      ​
      ​

    • Resolution for Scenario 1: Delete the incorrect on-premise Customer Promotion Zones and add the customer to the appropriate off-premise promotion zones. Ensure these zones are tied to the correct "Market" that aligns with the expected BudNet pricing.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  3. Investigate the "Legacy Frontline Zone" on the Distribution Area:
    ​
    ​

    • In Encompass, find the "Distribution Area" assigned to the customer(s) experiencing the exception.
      ​
      ​

    • Examine the "Legacy Frontline Zone" field within the Distribution Area settings.
      ​
      ​

    • Important Note: BudNet/VIPR uses the "Legacy Frontline Zone" on the Distribution Area to determine the expected pricing, regardless of how your actual pricing is calculated in Encompass.
      ​
      ​

    • Example Scenario 2 (Incorrect Legacy Zone): If a customer is set up correctly to receive the desired price, but the "Legacy Frontline Zone" on their Distribution Area is linked to a lower-priced promotion (either directly or through an attached Market), a VIPR exception will occur.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  4. Compare Encompass Invoice Data with BudNet Expected Pricing:
    ​
    ​

    • Review the relevant invoices in Encompass for the products and customers in the exception.
      ​
      ​

    • Use the Invoice Price Calculator in Encompass to understand how the final price was determined, including any applied promotions.
      ​
      ​

    • Compare the actual selling price on the invoice with the "expected" frontline price indicated by BudNet in the VIPR exception.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  5. Analyze Market and Promotion Configurations (If Necessary):
    ​
    ​

    • Understand how your Markets and Promotions are configured in Encompass and how they relate to your Customer Promotion Zones.
      ​
      ​

    • Verify that the Markets associated with your off-premise promotions are the ones BudNet expects for your off-premise customers (and vice versa for on-premise).
      ​
      ​

    • Caution: Making changes to Market and Promotion structures can have widespread effects. Proceed with caution and ensure you understand the implications.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  6. Consider Potential Resolutions Based on Legacy Frontline Zone:
    ​
    ​

    • Option 1: Change the "Legacy Frontline Zone": On the Distribution Area assigned to the customer, change the "Legacy Frontline Zone" to one that does not have lower-priced promotions associated with it (either directly or through a linked Market).
      ​
      ​

    • Option 2: Change the Distribution Area: Assign a different Distribution Area to the customer, one that already has a "Legacy Frontline Zone" that aligns with the pricing BudNet expects.
      ​
      ​
      ​

  7. If the Issue Persists, Contact Encompass Support:
    ​
    ​

    • If you have followed the above steps and are still experiencing VIPR exceptions, gather the following information to provide to Encompass Support for further assistance:
      ​
      ​

      • Product Description Codes (PDCNs) or ProductIDs involved.
        ​
        ​

      • The expected frontline price and discount from the BudNet VIPR report.
        ​
        ​

      • The frontline price being reported by Encompass (as seen on the invoice).
        ​
        ​

      • Any specific Markets and Promotion Zones you suspect might be involved
        ​
        ​

      • A clear description of the discrepancy and what pricing you expect BudNet to see.

Fields And Definitions

  • VIPR (Value In Price Reporting): A BudNet system for verifying and reporting pricing information.
    ​
    ​

  • PDCN (Product Description Code Number): A unique identifier for a product.
    ​
    ​

  • Frontline Price: The standard selling price of a product before any discounts or promotions.
    ​
    ​

  • On-Premise: Locations where alcoholic beverages are consumed on the premises (e.g., bars, restaurants).
    ​
    ​

  • Off-Premise: Locations where alcoholic beverages are purchased for consumption elsewhere (e.g., liquor stores, grocery stores).
    ​
    ​

  • Customer Promotion Zones: Configurable groupings of customers in Encompass that are assigned specific promotions and pricing.
    ​
    ​

  • Distribution Area: A geographical or logical grouping of customers in Encompass, which includes a "Legacy Frontline Zone" setting.
    ​
    ​

  • Legacy Frontline Zone: A setting within the Distribution Area in Encompass that BudNet/VIPR uses to determine the expected frontline price. It does not directly control pricing in Encompass but influences VIPR expectations.
    ​
    ​

  • Market: In Encompass, a higher-level grouping that can contain multiple Promotion Zones and is often tied to specific pricing strategies.
    ​
    ​

  • Promotion: A specific pricing offer or discount applied to products for certain customers or zones.
    ​
    ​

  • Exchange Task Files: Data files exchanged between Encompass and external systems like BudNet, containing pricing and other information.

Best Practices

  • Regularly Review Customer Promotion Zone Assignments: Ensure new and existing customers are placed in the correct zones based on their on-premise/off-premise status.
    ​
    ​

  • Understand the Relationship Between Distribution Areas and Legacy Frontline Zones: Be aware that this setting dictates the expected pricing in BudNet's VIPR reporting.
    ​
    ​

  • Maintain Consistent Market and Promotion Configurations: Ensure your Market and Promotion structures align with BudNet's expectations for on-premise and off-premise pricing.
    ​
    ​

  • Document Pricing Configurations: Keep records of your on-premise and off-premise pricing strategies and how they are configured within Encompass.
    ​
    ​

  • Proactively Address Pricing Changes: When implementing pricing changes, review the potential impact on VIPR reporting and adjust Encompass configurations accordingly.

16990013:
Distributor guide for when stops show up on routes or get pre-sell events in the wrong week: check stop phase, Pre-sell Days In Advance, next delivery date and the Date Conversions table. v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You are using a routing system where stops are assigned a phase (e.g., Phase 1, 2, 3, 4) that dictates when deliveries or pre-sells should occur.
    ​
    ​

  • You have observed that some stops are being included in a route or generating pre-sell events at an unexpected time based on their assigned phase.
    ​
    ​

  • You have access to the route configuration, stop details (including assigned phase and any pre-sell day settings), and potentially a date conversion table.

Steps

1. Identify the Affected Route(s) and Stops: Note the specific route numbers and stop IDs where you are seeing the unexpected phasing behavior.
​
2. Verify the Stop's Assigned Phase: Confirm the phase assigned to the affected stop(s) in your routing system.
​
3. Check the Pre-sell Days in Advance Setting: Determine the "Pre-sell Days In Advance" setting for the affected stop(s). Understand if this setting uses calendar days or business day calculations.
​
4. Determine the Next Scheduled Delivery Date: Identify the "Next Scheduled Delivery Date" for the affected stop(s).
​
5. Understand the Relationship Between Phase and Delivery Date: Recognize that in this system, Stops.Phase always relates to the Delivery Date Phase.
​
6. Consult the Date Conversions Table: Check which phase the "Next Scheduled Delivery Date" falls under. The pre-sell event generation is based on this delivery date's phase and the "Pre-sell Days In Advance" setting.
​
7. Example Analysis:

  • For a stop with a Presell Date of 3/5/2025 and a 2-day advance pre-sell, the Delivery Date is 3/7/2025. If 3/7/2025 falls into Phase Two according to the date conversions, then a pre-sell event for Phase Two would be generated.
    ​
    ​

  • For a stop with a Presell Date of 3/5/2025 and a 3-day advance pre-sell using business day calculations, the Delivery Date is 3/10/2025. If 3/10/2025 falls into Phase Three, then a pre-sell event for Phase Three would be generated.

8. Consider the Rolling 4-Week Cycle: Understand that phasing might operate on a rolling 4-week cycle based on a date conversions table. The phase assigned to a specific date determines when pre-sells occur.
​
9. If the issue persists, contact support: Provide the following information to the support team for further investigation:

  • The affected route number(s) and stop ID(s).
    ​
    ​

  • The expected behavior (when the stop should have been included in the route or when the pre-sell event should have been generated).
    ​
    ​

  • The actual behavior observed.
    ​
    ​

  • Screenshots or exports showing the stop's phase, pre-sell days in advance, and next scheduled delivery date.

Fields And Definitions

  • Stops.Phase: A field associated with each stop that indicates its assigned phase. In this system, it directly corresponds to the phase of the delivery date.
    ​
    ​

  • Presell Date: The date on which a pre-sell activity occurs.
    ​
    ​

  • Delivery Date: The scheduled date for the delivery to the stop. The phase of this date, according to the date conversions, determines the pre-sell event timing.
    ​
    ​

  • Pre-sell Days In Advance: The number of days before the delivery date that a pre-sell event is scheduled. This can be based on calendar days or business days.
    ​
    ​

  • Next Scheduled Date: The upcoming delivery date for a particular stop.
    ​
    ​

  • Date Conversions Table: A table that maps specific dates to their corresponding phase in the routing cycle. This table is crucial for understanding how the system determines the phase of a delivery date.
    ​
    ​

  • Business Day Calculations: When calculating pre-sell dates, this method only counts working days (typically excluding weekends and holidays).
    ​
    ​

  • Rolling 4-Week Cycle: A common phasing approach where the phases repeat every four weeks based on the calendar.

Best Practices

  • Ensure a clear understanding of how your system defines and applies phases, especially the relationship between the "Stops.Phase" and the delivery date.
    ​
    ​

  • If using "Pre-sell Days In Advance," be aware of whether it calculates based on calendar days or business days. Familiarize yourself with any date conversion tables used by your system to determine which phase a specific date falls under.
    ​
    ​

  • When setting up routes and stops, double-check the assigned phases and pre-sell day settings to avoid unexpected behavior.
    ​
    ​

  • If the expected phasing is based on specific weeks of the month (e.g., Phase 2 & 4 in the second and fourth week), confirm if your system's configuration aligns with this expectation, especially considering any rolling cycle logic.

  2. Create the Different Required Credit Terms:

16990016:
Explains Case Equivalents (CEs) in Encompass with a beer example converting cases and kegs to a standard 288 oz case to compare sales volume. Needs the Case Equivalents table set up. Requires v24.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 24.01

Pre-Conditions

  • Case Equivalents must be configured in the Case Equivalents table

Steps

Case Equivalent Definition:
​
​

A Case Equivalent (CE) is a standard unit used in sales to measure the total volume of a product sold, rather than just the number of individual items. This allows for a more accurate comparison of sales when products are sold in various sizes. For example, in the beer industry, a standard case is often defined as 288 ounces, and different packaging sizes are converted to this equivalent.

Example Breakdown:

Let's look at how Case Equivalents are used to compare beer sales for Brand A:
​
​

  • Standard Case: We know that one standard case of Brand A is equal to 288 ounces. This is our base unit for comparison.
    ​
    ​

  • Salesman X's Sales: Salesman X sold 10 cases of Brand A.
    ​
    -Since one case equals one case equivalent, Salesman X sold 10 Case Equivalents.
    ​
    ​

  • Salesman Y's Sales: Salesman Y sold 4 half-barrel kegs of Brand A.
    ​
    -One half-barrel keg contains approximately 1,984 ounces of beer.
    ​
    -To find out how many case equivalents that is, we divide the keg's ounces by the ounces in a standard case: 1984 ounces / 288 ounces/case = approximately 6.88 case equivalents per keg.
    ​
    -Since Salesman Y sold 4 kegs, his total case equivalents are: 4 kegs * 6.88 case equivalents/keg = 27.52 Case Equivalents (often rounded to 27.55).

​
In Summary:
​
Using Case Equivalents, we can see that even though Salesman X sold more individual packages (10 cases), Salesman Y sold significantly more beer in terms of total volume (27.55 case equivalents) because kegs contain a much larger quantity than cases. This standardized measurement provides a clearer picture of overall sales performance.

Best Practices

  • The case equivalents table should be configured as broadly as possible using the standard package size in ounces for a group of products.

16990018:
Admin guide to Table Triggers in Encompass: run Cloud Function code before or after records are added, edited, deleted or merged. Needs Cloud Function access and trigger permissions; v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Pre-Conditions

  • You must have access to create and edit Cloud Functions in Encompass
    ​
    ​

  • Your user account must have appropriate permissions to add table triggers
    ​
    ​

  • You need to understand the table structure, field names, and data types for the tables you want to trigger against
    ​
    ​

  • For triggers that modify data, appropriate update permissions are required on the target tables

Steps

Understanding Table Edit Triggers

Table Edit Triggers provide a way to execute custom code when specific operations occur on database tables within the Encompass system. The triggers can run before or after records are added, edited, or deleted, allowing you to implement business rules, validation, data synchronization, and automated workflows.

Trigger Types

Encompass supports seven types of triggers:

  • BeforeAdd (ID: 5) - Executes before a new record is added to a table
    ​
    ​

  • AfterAdd (ID: 1) - Executes after a new record has been added to a table
    ​
    ​

  • BeforeEdit (ID: 7) - Executes before changes to an existing record are saved
    ​
    ​

  • AfterEdit (ID: 2) - Executes after changes to an existing record have been saved
    ​
    ​

  • BeforeDelete (ID: 6) - Executes before a record is deleted
    ​
    ​

  • AfterDelete (ID: 3) - Executes after a record has been deleted
    ​
    ​

  • Merge (ID: 4) - Executes when records are merged

Creating a Table Trigger

1. Create a new Cloud Function in Encompass
​
2. Define the trigger logic in your code
​
3. Register your trigger with the system, specifying the table, trigger type, and field dependencies
​
- This is done on the Table Triggers table, attaching it to the table you want to trigger on.
​
4. Test your trigger to ensure it functions correctly

Trigger Execution Flow

1. When a table operation occurs (add, edit, delete), the Encompass system checks for registered triggers
​
2. For matching triggers, the system creates a TriggerParameter object with context information
​
3. Before triggers run immediately and can prevent the operation if validation fails
​
4. After triggers run once the database operation is completed
​
5. Asynchronous triggers run in the background without blocking the user's workflow
​
6. Triggers may be and are commonly batch executed, meaning that more than one record modification is added up, then the triggers are run all at once. This only applies to 'after' type triggers.

Fields And Definitions

Trigger Configuration Fields

  • TableName: The name of the table to watch for changes
    ​
    ​

  • TriggerTypeID: Numeric ID indicating when the trigger should fire (see Trigger Types above)
    ​
    ​

  • FieldList: Comma-separated list of fields that will activate the trigger when changed
    ​
    ​

  • APICommand: The name of the API command or function to execute
    ​
    ​

  • RunAsync: Boolean (0/1) indicating if the trigger should run asynchronously
    ​
    ​

  • Active: Boolean (0/1) indicating if the trigger is currently enabled

BC_TableTrigger.Trigger Structure

  • TableTriggerID: Unique identifier for the trigger
    ​
    ​

  • APICommand: The command to execute when the trigger fires
    ​
    ​

  • TriggerTypeID: The type of trigger (Before/After Add/Edit/Delete/Merge)
    ​
    ​

  • FieldArr: Array of field names that will activate the trigger
    ​
    ​

  • RunAsync: Whether the trigger should run in the background
    ​
    ​

  • Active: Whether the trigger is currently enabled

Best Practices

Performance Considerations

  • Minimize trigger chains: Avoid creating triggers that modify data which would trigger other triggers, as this can lead to performance issues and potential infinite loops.
    ​
    ​

  • Use field dependencies: Specify only the fields that should activate your trigger. This prevents unnecessary executions when unrelated fields are modified.
    ​
    ​

  • Use batch processing: Design triggers to handle multiple records efficiently rather than processing each record individually. Triggers are always executed in batch where they can in the Encompass code base for performance improvements, such as all Table Imports.

Error Handling

  • Validate input data: Always check for null values and validate data before use to prevent runtime errors.
    ​
    ​

  • Return clear error messages: When validation fails, provide specific error messages to help users understand the issue.
    ​
    ​

  • Avoid throwing exceptions in After triggers: Before triggers can validate and prevent operations, but After triggers should handle errors gracefully since the database operation has already completed.

Data Integrity

  • Be cautious with cascading updates: When implementing triggers that modify related records, ensure that your logic handles all edge cases.
    ​
    ​

  • Test thoroughly: Test your triggers with various scenarios, including edge cases and potential error conditions.

Security

  • Check permissions: Unless overriding permissions is necessary, ensure your trigger respects the user's permission level.
    ​
    ​

  • Limit trigger scope: Design triggers to execute only when necessary and with the minimum required permissions.

Maintenance

  • Document your triggers: Maintain documentation about what each trigger does, when it runs, and its dependencies.
    ​
    ​

  • Use meaningful names: Choose descriptive names for your triggers and related functions.
    ​
    ​

  • Keep triggers simple: Complex trigger logic is difficult to maintain. Consider breaking complex operations into smaller, more manageable pieces.
    ​
    ​

  • Test after upgrades: Re-test your triggers after system upgrades to ensure compatibility.
16990019:
Tips to make Table Import in Encompass faster: import only changed data, link on the primary ID, map only needed columns, use Bulk actions and optimize table triggers. Needs TableImport permission. v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Pre-Conditions

  • Table Import requires the TableImport permission to use
    ​
    ​

  • The Import Routine must belong to the current system to be editable

Steps

Introduction

This guide provides best practices for optimizing data imports using the Table Import engine. Following these recommendations will help improve import performance and reduce processing time.

Performance Optimization Techniques
​
​

Data Volume Management
​
​

  • Import Only Changed Data (DELTA): The single most important optimization is to only import records that have actually changed, rather than reimporting entire datasets. This "delta" approach dramatically reduces processing time.

Key Selection and Mapping
​
​

  • Link on Primary ID: Whenever possible, use the table's main ID field as the linking key rather than composite multi-column links. Single-column keys provide faster lookups and simpler processing.
    ​
    ​

  • Minimize Column Mapping: Only include columns that need updating in your import file. If including unnecessary columns can't be avoided, leave these unmapped in the field mapping interface to prevent wasteful processing.

Processing Options
​
​

  • Utilize Bulk Actions: For custom tables where field audits or triggers aren't required, enable the 'Bulk' action options. This allows for much faster data processing by bypassing row-by-row operations.

System Integration Considerations
​
​

  • Optimize Table Triggers: If the target table has custom triggers, review and optimize these trigger scripts to ensure they execute efficiently during large imports. Inefficient triggers can dramatically slow down the import process.

Conclusion

By applying these optimization techniques to your Table Import operations, you'll significantly improve import speeds and reduce system resource consumption. For assistance with complex import scenarios, consult with your data team.

Troubleshooting for "Out of Stock" showing on invoices with returns: check backorder vs delivered quantity, Auto Backorder on the reason code, and customer history audit, plus what to send Support. Requires v22.01+.

Distributor steps to charge and track sales tax on samples in Encompass: invoice a dedicated Samples customer without zero-dollar promos, then clear the balance with an AR write-off product. Requires v25.01+.

    ​

    ​
    ​

    ​
    ​

  • Edit the promotion(s) to either remove the sample customer as a qualifier or set an end date for the promotion.

    ​

    ​
    ​

  • Ensure all products and quantities for the samples are accurately entered on the invoice.
    ​
    ​

  • The system should now calculate the applicable sales tax based on your standard tax settings for this customer.

3. Create a non-inventory product for Accounts Receivable (AR) Write-Offs.

  • Navigate to the Products table in Encompass.
    ​
    ​

  • Create a new non-inventory product (e.g., "A/R Write Off - Samples").

    ​

-Important: Ensure there is an Income Account Map set up for the Income Area associated with samples. This mapping is crucial for generating the correct entries to your tax liability accounts.

    ​

    ​

    ​

5. If the issue persists after following these steps, please contact Encompass Support and provide the following information for efficient troubleshooting:

    ​

Best Practices

A Case Equivalent (CE) is a standard unit used in sales to measure the total volume of a product sold, rather than just the number of individual items. This allows for a more accurate comparison of sales when products are sold in various sizes. For example, in the beer industry, a standard case is often defined as 288 ounces, and different packaging sizes are converted to this equivalent.

Example Breakdown:

Let's look at how Case Equivalents are used to compare beer sales for Brand A:

Standard Case: We know that one standard case of Brand A is equal to 288 ounces. This is our base unit for comparison.

Salesman X's Sales: Salesman X sold 10 cases of Brand A.

- Since one case equals one case equivalent, Salesman X sold 10 Case Equivalents.

Salesman Y's Sales: Salesman Y sold 4 half-barrel kegs of Brand A.

- One half-barrel keg contains approximately 1,984 ounces of beer.

- To find out how many case equivalents that is, we divide the keg's ounces by the ounces in a standard case: 1984 ounces / 288 ounces/case = approximately 6.88 case equivalents per keg.

- Since Salesman Y sold 4 kegs, his total case equivalents are: 4 kegs * 6.88 case equivalents/keg = 27.52 Case Equivalents (often rounded to 27.55).

In Summary:

Using Case Equivalents, we can see that even though Salesman X sold more individual packages (10 cases), Salesman Y sold significantly more beer in terms of total volume (27.55 case equivalents) because kegs contain a much larger quantity than cases. This standardized measurement provides a clearer picture of overall sales performance.

Best Practices

  • The case equivalents table should be configured as broadly as possible using the standard package size in ounces for a group of products.

16990031:
Tips to speed up slow or timing-out Fusion reports in Encompass: trim columns, add default filters, flatten queries, use join pruning and the Explain tab, and how timeout disabling works. Needs Fusion Edit. v22.03+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.03

Pre-Conditions

  • Required Fusion Edit permission to be able to edit fusion reports, to optimize them.
    ​
    ​

  • You must be the owner of the report you would like to optimize to save back to the original report ID

Steps

Introduction

This guide provides best practices for optimizing reports in the Fusion reporting engine to improve performance, reduce timeouts, and enhance user experience.

Performance Optimization Techniques
​
​

Always start with...
​
​

Simplify the business case: Reports tend to grow in complexity over time; columns, filters, and options being added as new needs arise. Likely, consumers of your report are only looking at 2-3 columns on a daily basis, everything else may be clutter.
​
The largest performance gains are often found by checking that old items are still needed, removing columns (and related joins) and filters will both improve performance, and simplify/improve the experience for the consumer of your report. Things can always be added back later.

Report Structure Optimization

  • Break Down Large Reports: Split complex reports into smaller, focused reports to improve processing time and maintainability. Add multiple reports to a dashboard if you need to see the data together. Utilize dashboard tabs to break up large dashboards into smaller, more consumable sets.
    ​
    ​

  • Reduce Complex Expressions: Simplify calculations and expressions where possible to minimize processing overhead.
    ​
    ​

  • Flatten Query Structure: Eliminate sub-queries and sub-reports whenever possible. Most SQL queries can be restructured into a single layer. Consider using an AI LLM to help optimize complex query structures, you can copy the SQL from the 'Show Report SQL' tab and ask an AI to "reduce down to a single layer query without any sub-queries or CTEs".

Data Volume Management

  • Use Default Filters: Always configure default filters to prevent unfiltered report executions that can cause timeouts.
    ​
    ​

  • Filter Early on Date Ranges: Apply date range filters as early as possible in your query to limit the amount of data being processed.
    ​
    ​

  • Limit Row Returns: Configure your report to return only the necessary number of rows. Large result sets significantly impact performance.
    ​
    ​

  • Leverage Filters and Drill-Downs: Utilize these features to allow users to narrow down data as needed rather than loading everything at once.

Join Optimization

  • Enable "Join Required = False": Where appropriate, use this setting for joins in your report. This allows the Fusion engine to implement automatic join-pruning, only including joins when they're needed for user-selected filters or drill-downs.

Advanced Performance Tuning

  • Use the "Explain" Tab: When editing reports, check the Explain tab to view the Snowflake query profile. This helps identify which nodes are scanning the most data, allowing you to target optimization efforts. Filter these node more to reduce data scanning.
    ​
    ​

  • Avoid Pivoting Features: Minimize use of Child/Detail/Column/Column Totals features. When these are enabled, the report runs as a 'PIVOT' or 'ROLLUP' operation, which is significantly slower than standard queries.

Report Timeout Disable Behavior

Reports in Encompass that run beyond the timeout are marked as a timeout.

Reports that timeout are disabled using an exponential timeout calculation.
​
The equation is: 10 minutes * (2 ^ Fail Count)
​
​For example:

  • 1 failure = disabled for 20 minutes
    ​
    ​

  • 2 failures = disabled for 40 minutes
    ​
    ​

  • 3 failures = disabled for 80 minutes
    ​
    ​

  • 4 failures = disabled for 160 minutes (2.7 hours)
    ​
    ​

  • 5 failures = disabled for 320 minutes (5.3 hours)
    ​
    ​

  • 6 failures = disabled for 640 minutes (10.7 hours)
    ​
    ​

  • 7 failures = disabled for 1280 minutes (21.3 hours)
    ​
    ​

  • 8 failures = disabled for 2560 minutes (42.6 hours)
    ​
    ​

  • 9 failures = disabled for 5120 minutes (3.6 days)
    ​
    ​

  • 10 failures = disabled for 10240 minutes (7.1 days)
    ​
    ​

  • continued...

This behavior is part of the limitless capabilites of Fusion reporting, and ensures that no single report causes slowness for all other users of the system.

Distributor guide to the Fusion Forecast vs. Actual report in Encompass (report 20897287): weekly or monthly forecast vs this year and last year sales by supplier, filters and column definitions. v25.04+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.04

Steps

The fusion version of the Forecast vs. Actual Report can currently be run by running report id 20897287. This will be added to the report library soon.

    ​

  1. After the report renders, click on a supplier to see the drill-down options

  2. Click on the filters tab to add additional filters or to change to monthly periods.
    ​
    ​

  3. Click on the layout tab to add additional group by columns.

Fields And Definitions

Parameters/Filters:
​
​

  • Period Type: Weeks (Default) or Months. This will filter on weekly or monthly forecast data.
    ​
    ​

  • Forecast Group: Filters on inventory records belonging to a certain forecast group (Inventory - Forecast Group Effective)
    ​
    ​

  • Purchase Agent: Filters on the purchase agent for a forecast group (Forecast Groups - Purchase Agent)
    ​
    ​

  • Supplier: Filters on products for the selected suppliers (Products - Supplier)
    ​
    ​

  • Brand Family: Filters on products for the selected brand families (Products > Brands > Brand Families)
    ​
    ​

  • Brand: Filters on products for the selected brands (Product > Brands)
    ​
    ​

  • Product: Filters on selected products.

  • Start Date: Filters on the weekly or monthly start date of a forecast period. Weekly forecasts periods start on either a Sunday or Monday depending on setting 56, so if running the forecast period = weekly, the start date will either be a Sunday or Monday. For example, if setting 56 = Monday and the Start Date entered = Wednesday, 3/5/2025, the start date used by the report will be Monday, 3/3/2025. If the start date is left empty, the report will run for the previous weekly or monthly period.
    ​
    ​

  • End Date: Filters on the weekly or monthly end date of a forecast period. Weekly forecasts periods end on either a Saturday or Sunday depending on setting 56, so if running the forecast period = weekly, the end date will either be a Sunday or Monday. For example, if setting 56 = Monday and the End Date entered = Wednesday, 3/5/2025, the end date used by the report will be Sunday, 3/9/2025. If the end date is left empty, the report will run for the previous weekly or monthly period.
    ​
    ​

Columns / Values:
​

  • Period: This will show the forecast period date range based on the start and end date entered. If the start and end dates are left empty, the report will run for the previous weekly or monthly period.
    ​
    ​

  • Forecasted Sales: Forecasted sales for the period. This value will include the system forecasted values unless a user has entered a forecast value.
    ​
    ​

  • This Year Sales: Sales for the current year for sale customer account types in the forecast period unless, an invoice transaction has been excluded or the customer type is not included in sales forecast.
    ​
    ​

  • Remaining: Difference forecasted sales compared to this year sales. Forecasted Sales - This Year Sales
    ​
    ​

  • Remaining%: Remaining percentage of Forecasted vs actual. (Forecasted Sales - This Year Sales) / Forecast
    ​
    ​

  • Last Year Sales: Sales for the previous year for sale customer account types in the forecast period, unless an invoice transaction has been excluded or the customer type is not included in sales forecast.
    ​
    ​

  • Diff Last Year: Difference in actual sales compared to the previous year. This Year Sales - Last Year Sales
    ​
    ​

  • Diff Last Year %: Percentage difference in actual sales compared to the previous year. (This Year Sales - Last Year Sales) / This Year Sales
    ​
    ​

  • Forecast Variance: Accuracy of the forecasted sales compared to actual sales. This will be displayed in absolute values only. (This Year Sales - Forecasted Sales) / This Year Sales

16990037:
Distributor explainer of route phasing in Encompass: stop phase follows the delivery date on a rolling 4-week Date Conversions cycle, with business-day presell examples and troubleshooting. v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Pre-Conditions

Introduction
​
​This document explains how route phasing works in Encompass and provides troubleshooting steps for issues where stops are included in a route when they should not be, due to perceived phasing errors.


Understanding Route Phasing
​
​

  • Delivery Date Phasing:
    ​
    ​

    • In Encompass, "Stops.Phase" always refers to the Delivery Date Phase.
      ​
      ​

    • Phasing operates on a rolling 4-week cycle, determined by the "Date Conversions" table.
      ​
      ​

    • The phase assigned to a stop is based on its delivery date, not the presell date.
      ​
      ​

  • Presell and Delivery Dates:
    ​
    ​

    • The presell date determines when a salesperson can create an order.
      ​
      ​

    • The delivery date determines which phase the stop falls into.
      ​
      ​

    • The system uses business day calculations to determine the delivery date based on the presell date and the lead time (e.g., 2-day or 3-day presell).
      ​
      ​

  • Date Conversions Table:
    ​
    ​

    • The "Date Conversions" table is the definitive source for determining which phase a specific date falls under.

Steps

Troubleshooting Steps
​
​

1. Verify Presell and Delivery Dates:
​

  • Confirm the presell and delivery dates for the stops in question.
    ​
    ​

  • Ensure that the lead time (presell days) is correctly calculated using business day calculations.
    ​
    ​

2. Check the Date Conversions Table:

  • Use the "Date Conversions" table to determine which phase the delivery date falls under.
    ​
    ​

  • This will confirm if the system is correctly assigning the phase.
    ​
    ​

3. Addressing Misunderstandings:

  • Clarify Phasing Concept: Phasing is based on a rolling 4-week cycle determined by delivery dates.
    ​
    ​

  • Explain Business Day Calculations: All deliveries must fall on a day that is set to is business day = true on the date conversions table. If a day is set to is business day = false, the system will skip that day.
    ​
    ​

4. Provide Information to Support:

  • When reporting a phasing issue, provide the following:
    ​
    ​

    • Route number.
      ​
      ​

    • Stop IDs.
      ​
      ​

    • Presell dates.
      ​
      ​

    • Delivery dates.
      ​
      ​

    • Screen shots of the date conversion table if possible.

Fields And Definitions

Example Scenario:
​
​

  • Scenario: A stop with a 2-day presell has a presell date of 3/5/2025.
    ​
    ​

  • Delivery Date Calculation: The delivery date is calculated as 3/7/2025 (2 days after 3/5/2025).
    ​
    ​

  • Phase Determination: Check the "Date Conversions" table for 3/7/2025. If 3/7/2025 falls into Phase 2, the stop will be assigned to Phase 2.
    ​
    ​

  • 3 day presell example: If a stop has a 3 day presell, then the delivery date is calculated using business day calculations. So if the presell date is 3/5/2025, then the delivery date would be 3/10/2025.

Best Practices

Important Notes

  • Always refer to the "Date Conversions" table to confirm phase assignments.
    ​
    ​

  • Understand that presell and delivery dates are distinct and serve different purposes.
    ​
    ​

  • Business day calculations will effect the delivery date.
    ​
    ​

  • If you are unsure of any of these steps, please contact Encompass support.

16990041:
Explains why Encompass stops sending emails to addresses on the email suppression list (marked as spam or bounced) and how to check the reason in the Messages table. For distributors not receiving system emails.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Steps

Overview

Email suppression lists are an important part of our email delivery system that helps maintain our sending reputation and ensures compliance with email best practices. This article explains what suppression lists are, and why email addresses get added to them.

What is an Email Suppression List?

A suppression list contains email addresses that our system will not send emails to. These addresses are automatically added to this list when certain conditions are met, helping to protect our email sender reputation.
​
​

Email addresses are added to our suppression lists for two primary reasons:

  1. Marked as SPAM - The recipient has explicitly marked our communications as spam
    ​
    ​

  2. Invalid Email (Bounced) - The email address is not valid, resulting in a bounce

You can verify the specific reason an email was rejected by checking the messages table, where the rejected message will indicate the failure reason.

Impact of Suppression Lists

When an email address is on a suppression list:

  • Encompass will not attempt to deliver emails to that address
    ​
    ​

  • This helps maintain our overall email deliverability and sender reputation
    ​
    ​

  • It ensures compliance with email sending best practices

What This Means for You

If you're not receiving expected emails from the system, your email address might be on the suppression list. This could happen if:

  • Your email account previously didn't exist or was full
    ​
    ​

  • You or someone with access to your email account marked our messages as spam
    ​
    ​

  • Your email server previously rejected our messages

Best Practices

  • Prioritize maintaining a good sender reputation by not over expanding your recipient list
    ​
    ​

  • Consider alternative communication methods for contacts who have marked emails as spam

16990050:
Distributor guide to Product Ranking Codes (AA-DD) in Encompass: how ABC thresholds for cases and dollars are set and calculated for PO Generator and purchasing. Requires v25.03+ and setting 3306 enabled.

Minimum Version Required: 25.03

Pre-Conditions

Global Settings:

  • Product Ranking will be calculated based on the product requirements listed below, however, in order to display product ranking codes within PO Generator, setting 3306 - Enable Product Ranking Codes for Forecasting must be set to True.
    ​
    ​

  • Review Forecast Locations to confirm your configuration for ranking period and ABC percentage thresholds
    ​
    ​

  • Percentage A - D must equal 100
    ​
    ​

  • Forecast Locations - Create Forecast Records = True

Product Requirements:

  • Products must be on a verified invoice during the ranking period for Sale account type customers
    ​
    ​

  • Products must belong to a forecast group
    ​
    ​

  • Products have to be in a product type where Include in Sales Reports by Default = True

Steps

Business Case:

Product Ranking Codes can be used for fulfillment reporting, prioritization of purchasing and warehouse management.

Ranking Percentages:

Rankings will be based on the cumulative totals for cases and dollars sold using the A, B, C, and D thresholds described below.
​
​

  • Percentage A: These are the products in the top the "A" percentage of total cases or dollars sold for the location. For example, if percentage A = 80, this is the top 80% of total cases or dollars.
    ​
    ​

  • Percentage B: These products represent the next "B" percentage of total cases and dollars sold for the location. For example, if B is 10 and percentage A is 80, then B products contribute to the next 10-20% of the cumulative total.
    ​

  • Percentage C: These products represent the next "C" percentage of total cases or dollars sold for the location. For example, if C is 5 and percentage B is 10, then C products contribute to the next 5-10% of the cumulative total.
    ​

  • Percentage D: The bottom percentage or the remaining products represent the bottom "D" percentage of cases sold. For example, if D is 5, then D products contribute to the last 5% of your total cases sold.

-When setting the percentage ranking thresholds. The total of A - D should add up to 100.
​
-Default values set by the system are A - 80, B - 10, C - 5, D - 5.

Other thresholds examples could be:
​
​

  • A - 90, B - 5, C - 3, D - 2 (A is Top 90%, B is the next 5 - 10%, C is the next 3 - 5%, and D is the remaining 2%)
    ​
    ​

  • A - 75, B - 15, C - 5, D - 5 (A is Top 75%, B is the next 15 - 25%, C is the next 5 - 15%, and D is the remaining 5%)
    ​

  • A - 60, B - 30, C - 5, D - 5 (A is Top 60%, B is the next 30 - 40%, C is the next 5 - 30%, and D is the remaining 5%)

Product Ranking Codes:

Product Ranking Codes are two-dimensional, giving users the insights for both cases and dollars with a single ranking. The possible values are AA, AB, AC, AD, BA, BB, BC, BD, CA, CB, CC, CD, DA, DB, DC, DD. Each product is given a 2-character ranking code. The first letter is for volume or cases, the second letter is for sales dollars. So a BA product has a B ranking for case sold and an A ranking for $ volume.

How often are Product Ranking Codes updated?

The Set_ProductRankingCodes scheduled task will run weekly on Fridays at 10:00 pm

How Product Ranking Codes are calculated

The following examples will use 80, 10, 5, 5 for the A, B, C, D percentages respectively.

Step 1: Calculate Total Cases Sold and $Vol

  • Calculate the total cases sold and $vol across all qualified invoices and products based on the Forecast Locations Ranking Period. Options include 3, 4, 6, and 12 months.

Step 2: Sort products by Units Sold

  • Sort the products in descending order of Cases sold. This ranking will allow you to determine which products are in the top 80%, next 10-20%, and so on.
    ​
    ​

  • The same will be done for $Vol

Step 3: Calculate Percentile Cutoffs

Once sorted the products, the system will determine the cutoffs for each category:
​
​

  • Category A (Top 80%): These are the products with the highest sales volume (the top 80% of your total cases sold).
    ​
    ​

  • Category B (Next 10-20%): These products represent the next 10-20% of total cases sold.
    ​

  • Category C (Next 5-10%): These products represent the next 5-10% of total cases sold.
    ​

  • Category D (Bottom 5%): The remaining products represent the bottom 5% of cases sold.

Step 4: Assign Categories (A, B, C, D)

16990051:
Distributor setup to auto-create transfers from a multi-location forecast in Encompass: PO Generator purchases with transfer-to locations become transfer invoices on receipt, plus failure alerts. v26.05+.

Minimum Version Required: 26.05

Pre-Conditions

  • Forecast Group must have a Receive Location set.

  • Forecast Group must have inventory records for non-receive location
    ​
    ​

  • Transfer Planner Setup must be completed. See help resources to learn about setting up Transfer Planner
    ​
    ​

  • Purchases must be generated through the PO Generator.
    ​
    ​

  • Shipments Status must be Received, Confirmed, or Verified.

  • Purchase must be received after the Last Success Time of the Auto Transfers From Transfer To Purchase Trans scheduled task (ReceiveTime > LastSuccessTime)

  • The sum of the ordered and received quantity must equal, which is to say, SUM(PurchaseTrans.Ordered) = SUM(PurchaseTrans.NumUnits)

Steps

Generate Purchase Orders:
​
​

  • Use the PO Generator to create purchases for products intended to meet demand for other locations.
    ​
    ​

  • As shown below, the purchase will have transactions with the transfer to location set for other locations
    ​
    ​

    Screenshot

  • Important Step! Review the PO and update the status to "Ordered" once it has been sent to the supplier or vendor.

How the Automated Transfer is created:
​
​1. Once the shipment is received in the "primary" location, the Auto Transfers From Transfer To Purchase Trans scheduled task will run within 15 minutes and a transfer invoice will be created for the "primary" location
​
2. In order for the transfer invoice to be created, the following conditions must be met:

  • The shipment must be received
    ​
    ​

  • The total ordered must equal the total (num units) received for the entire purchase.
    ​
    ​

  • It is important to point out that products that are not included in sales reporting (Product Types - Include in Sales Reports by Default = False) will be ignored. This means that if dunnage products, such as empty pallets are added to the purchase during receiving, that will not prevent the transfer from being created.

3. The transfer invoice will have a Load Sheet date = The default will be the Receive Date + 1 business day, however the routing method associated with the transfer routes used.
​
4. The transfer purchase for the "other" locations will be created using the existing transfer planner EDI logic.
​
5. Once the transfer invoice is created, the transfer to location will be cleared out on the original purchase. This is to prevent duplicate transfers from being created.

Alerting

If for some reason the automated transfer does not get created, users can set up and subscribe to an Uncreated Transfer Notification alert.

  • Go to the alerts table and filter on alert type = 47) Uncreated Transfers Notification
    ​
    ​

  • If there is not an alert with alert type 47, create a new alert
    ​
    ​

  • Click the Sub Table button and select Alert Users
    ​
    ​

  • Click Add Alert Users

In most cases, the alert will be sent if the purchases is in received status and the total amount ordered does not match the total amount received.

Fields And Definitions

  • PO Generator: A tool that generates Purchase Orders based on demand forecasts.
    ​
    ​

  • Primary Location: The main location designated to receive purchased products.
    ​
    ​

  • Other Locations: Additional locations where there is demand for products.
    ​
    ​

  • Transfer To Transactions: Transactions representing the movement of inventory from the primary location to other designated locations.

16990054:
Brewery setup in Encompass for the TTB Brewers Report of Operations (BRO): tax entities, locations, product type TTB process types, brand TTB categories, and taproom/contract customer tax codes. v22.12+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.12

Pre-Conditions

  • This document will guide users through the configuration of a Manufacturer site on ECP to ensure accurate representation of all beer production and removal data required for the Federal TTB Brewers Report of Operations

Steps

Setting up Tax Entities
​
​

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Tax Entities table
​
2. Select Add Tax Entities
​
​

  • NOTE: You will need to add a separate Tax Entity for every active TTB Brewer’s Notice license your organization holds

3. Enter the following information:

  • Tax Entity - The name of the facility that holds the Brewer’s Notice
    ​
    ​

  • License Number - Your Brewer’s Notice license number
    ​
    ​

  • FEIN - Your Federal Employer Identification Number
    ​
    ​

4. Click Save Records

Configuring Locations

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Locations table
​
2. Hover over the Tax Entity column and click the edit pencil
​
3. Select the correct Tax Entity(s) for each location
​
4. Click Save Records

Configuring Product Types

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Product Types table

  • The common Product Types that we will want to configure for reporting on the TTB BRO Report are Finished Goods (cans, bottles, kegs, etc.) and Bright Beer

2. Set the TTB Process Type on the appropriate Product Type

NOTE: Your site’s Product Type naming conventions may differ

  • For Product Type: FG - Bottles you will chose TTB Process Type = Bottled
    ​
    ​

  • For Product Type: FG - Cans you will chose TTB Process Type = Canned
    ​
    ​

  • For Product Type: FG - Kegs you will chose TTB Process Type = Racked
    ​
    ​

  • For Product Type: WIP - Bright Beer you will chose TTB Process Type = Produced
    ​
    ​

3. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Locations Product Types table
​
4. Set the correct Tax Entity on the Product Type to correspond with your Location(s)

Configuring Brands

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Brands table
​
2. Ensure all of your Brands are categorized correctly under the ‘TTB Category’ column
​
3. For all beer Brands, choose the TTB Category: Beer
​
​

  • Note: The TTB defines beer as the following: Beer, ale, porter, stout, and other similar fermented beverages (including saké and similar products) of any name or description – containing one-half of one percent or more of alcohol by volume – brewed or produced from malt, wholly or in part, or from any substitute for malt.

4.For all non alcoholic beer Brands, choose the TTB Category: Cereal Beverage - Below .5% ABV
​
​

  • Note: The TTB defines non alcoholic beer as the following: A beverage, produced either wholly or in part from malt (or a substitute for malt), and either fermented or unfermented, which contains, when ready for consumption, less than one-half of 1 percent (0.5%) of alcohol by volume. Substitutes for malt are rice, grain of any kind, bran, glucose, sugar, and molasses.

Configuring Customers

Customers can be categorized with a TTB Tax Code that the BRO will pull data from. For initial TTB reporting configuration, we will want to ensure the proper Tax Code is set for the tavern on brewery premises (the taproom) as well as any contract brewing partners that receive beer from the facility without payment of tax.

Setting up Tavern on Brewery Premises Customers

If your brewery is classified as a ‘brewpub’ or contains a ‘tavern on brewery premises’, you will need to set up the relevant Customer record through the following steps:
​
​

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Customers table
​
2. Select the Customer that represents your tavern on brewery premises
​
3. On the TTB Tax Code field, select Tavern on Brewery Premises and click save

Setting up Contract Partner Customers for Beer Removed Without Payment of Tax

If your brewery produces beer for another brewery Customer of the same or different ownership and you will not be tax liable for these removals, you will need to set up these Customers through the following steps:

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Customers table
​
2. Select the Customer that you invoice beer to without payment of tax
​
3. On the TTB Tax Code field, select Removed Without Payment of Tax to Other Breweries and click save
​
​

  • Note: If these Customers also receive tax paid removals from your brewery, an additional customer must be added to reflect this

Setting up Contract Partner Vendors for Beer Received in Bond

If your brewery purchases beer in bond from another brewery to be taxed upon removal from your facility, you will need to set up these Vendors through the following steps:

1. Using Universal Search, navigate to the Vendors table
​
2. Select the Vendor that you invoice beer to without payment of tax
​
3. On the TTB Tax Code field, select Received In Bond and click save

Fields And Definitions

Tax Entities - The manufacturing facility represented by your Brewer’s Notice

Product Types - The term which describes a specific group of Products

  • TTB Process Type: Bottled and TTB Process Type: Canned will both report as ‘Bottling’ on the BRO
    ​
    ​

  • TTB Process Type: Racked will report under the ‘Racking’ columns on the BRO (aka: kegged finished goods)

Brands - For the BRO, the Brands table will allow you to define the TTB Category

  • TTB Category: ‘Beer’ should be used for all beer brands
    ​
    ​

  • TTB Category: ‘Cereal Beverage - Below .5% ABV’ should be used for all non-alcoholic beer brands

Best Practices

  • All Load Sheets must be in ‘Balanced’ Status to accurately reflect removals data for the BRO date period chosen
    ​
    ​

  • When adding new Brands, ensure that you set the correct TTB Brand Category brands without a TTB Brand Category will be omitted from the BRO
16990055:
Distributor admin guide for users who can't log in to Encompass (e.g. inactive user error): confirm active status, reset password, clear cache and fix duplicate email or Primary Encompass ID issues. v22.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 22.01

Pre-Conditions

    • Access to user administration settings within the Encompass system.

Steps

  1. Verify User Reactivation:

    • Check User Status: First and foremost, verify that the user's account is indeed marked as "active" in the system. Navigate to the user administration section and confirm the user's current status.

    • If the user is still marked as inactive, reactivate the account again, ensuring all required fields are correctly filled.

    • If the user was reactivated, verify that the reactivation was saved.

  2. General User Troubleshooting:

    • Password Reset: Have the user attempt to reset their password. There may be a password issue.

    • Browser/Cache: Have the user clear their browser cache and cookies or try a different browser.

    • System Outage: Confirm there are no system wide outages.

  3. Identify Email Addresses:

    • The email address they are using should be tied to the user record they are trying to log in to. We would also recommend checking the authentication record on their user record to ensure the primary encompass ID is set correctly.

  4. Gather Information:

    • Obtain the user's username or Encompass ID.

    • If possible, gather a screenshot of the error message the user is receiving.

  5. Investigate Email Address Usage:

    • Determine where else the user's email address is being used within the Encompass system.

    • This may involve searching for other user records, customer records, or any other entities that might be linked to the email address.

  6. Resolve Email Address Conflicts:

    • This is the most critical step, and the exact approach may vary depending on how the email address is being used. Here are some potential strategies:

      • Option 1 (Ideal, but may not be feasible):

        • The best practice is to assign unique email addresses to each user.

        • If possible, update the conflicting records to use a different email address. This will allow the reactivated user's Primary Encompass ID to update correctly.

      • Option 2 (If email address cannot be changed):

        • This option is more complex and should be approached with caution.

        • It may involve temporarily manipulating the email address associated with the reactivated user to force an update of the Primary Encompass ID.

        • Caution: This option should only be performed by personnel with a strong understanding of the Encompass system’s user management and authentication processes.

  7. Test User Login:

    • After resolving the email address conflicts, have the user attempt to log in.

    • Verify that the user is able to access the system without the "inactive user" error message.

Fields And Definitions

  • Primary Encompass ID: A unique identifier associated with a user account within the Encompass system.

  • User Record: The database record containing user information, including email address, status (active/inactive), and Encompass IDs.

  • Authentication: The process of verifying a user's identity to grant access to the system.

Best Practices

  • Unique Email Addresses:

    • Enforce a policy of using unique email addresses for each user account. This prevents conflicts and simplifies user management.

  • User Management Procedures:

    • Establish clear procedures for user management, including:

      • Account creation

      • Account reactivation

      • Account deactivation

      • Email address changes

  • Setting the users password

    • If you are unable to resolve the issues and the user cannot log in, you can remove their email address and phone number on the user record to set the password for them.

  • Error Message Collection:

    • When reporting user login issues, always collect the exact error message the user is receiving. This information is crucial for troubleshooting.

  • System Testing:

    • After making any changes to user accounts or authentication settings, thoroughly test the login process to ensure that users are able to access the system correctly.

  • Support Contact:

    • If you are unable to resolve the issue, contact Encompass support for assistance. They can provide specific guidance based on your system configuration.

    ​

    ​

How to create new Pick Rule(s) for the new Pick Method(s)

  1. Go to the Pick Rules table

    ​

  2. Filter to any Pick Rules that are used to pick ASN customers

Fields And Definitions

  • Load Group - Table holding configurations that determine what actions occur for a pallet throughout its picking lifecycle.

    ​

  • Pick Method - Table holding configurations that determine how a pallet is built, and how a user will interact with that pallet during picking.
    ​
    ​

  • Pick Rule - Table holding configurations that help identify groupings of products on invoices that should be assigned the same Pick Method during palletization.
    ​
    ​

  • Pick Team - A group of employees that are assigned to certain Pick Methods during the picking process. For example, a layer pick team or a keg pick team.
    ​
    ​

  • Customer Pick Type - Used to group certain customers together that need to have their orders built in a certain way.

Best Practices

  • Do not make any changes to Pick Rules, Pick Methods, or Load Groups without first considering the greater context of those changes. The steps in this article should not be followed verbatim; make sure you are referencing current warehouse processes and pick rule configurations to properly fit any new Costco-related records into the larger workflow.
    ​
    ​

  • Make sure to prioritize any new pick rules so that they fit within the current picking priorities during palletization. A priority that is too high or too low may interfere with non-Costco pallets, or result in Costco pallets not being labeled properly.
    ​
    ​

  • Make sure new Costco Pick Methods are added to a Pick Team, that way warehouse team members are allowed to pick the pallets.

16990063:
Producer guide to WIP accounting in Encompass OCloud: set up Production Stage Groups so raw material value moves through WIP accounts (Wort, Green, Bright) during production. Requires v23.06+.

Minimum Version Required: 23.06

Pre-Conditions

  • Applies to all OCloud producers.
    ​
    ​

  • Impacts all non-Packaging type Recipes/Production Orders.

Steps

Click here for documentation with screenshots

Value Statement:

Enable GAAP compliant WIP accounting visibility by creating accounting transactions throughout the production process.
​
​

Requirements:

  • Applies to all OCloud producers
    ​
    ​

  • Impacts all non-Packaging type Recipes/Production Orders


​
Problem Statement:

Prior to 23.06 (June 2023), Production Orders passed the value of consumed raw materials to a WIP Account at the time of completing the Production Order. This meant that the value of consumed raw materials was not passed to a WIP Account while the Production Order was in process. This resulted in an overstated Raw Materials Inventory Account and an understated WIP Account while the Production Order was in process. This was most impactful when using multi-stage Recipes/Production Orders that cover the brewing process from mash-to-bright beer, which typically takes between 2-4 weeks to fully complete.

The brewing industry standard is to break the production process into three common phases: Wort WIP -> Green Beer WIP -> Bright Beer WIP, and pass the value of all consumed raw materials to WIP Accounts for each production phase.


​
The Solution:

  • Allow defining production phases using Production Stage Groups.
    ​
    ​

  • Pass the value of consumed raw materials to WIP Accounts for each phase of production.
    ​
    ​

  • Minimize Recipe setup by auto-creating WIP Products for each Production Stage Group.
    ​
    ​
    ​

About Production Stage Groups

The purpose of Production Stage Groups is to define the phase(s) of the production process and temporarily store the value of all consumed ingredients in a WIP Account for each phase while the Production Order is in process.

Production Stage Groups define the phase(s) of the production process by associating Production Stage Types to a production phase. This is achieved by assigning Production Stage Types to a Production Stage Group.


​
How Production Stage Groups work with Recipes & Recipe Stages

Recipes consist of one or multiple Recipe Stages. Every Recipe Stage is assigned to a Production Stage Type and every Production Stage Type is assigned to a Production Stage Group.
​
​

The system auto-generates a WIP Product for each Recipe Stage based on the Production Stage Groups + Recipe Brand. The WIP Product is used to store the value of consumed raw materials in a WIP Account. The consumed raw material value is passed from one WIP Product to the next WIP Product as the brew moves through each production phase (e.g. Wort WIP -> Green Beer WIP).
​
​
​

How consumed raw material value flows through WIP accounts while a Production Order is in process

Every Recipe Stage has an assigned WIP Product, and Recipe Stages have raw materials consumed in each stage. Raw material value is passed to the WIP Account mapped to the Recipe Stage’s WIP Product when the raw material is consumed. The value of the WIP Account increases as each raw material is consumed.

WIP products map to a WIP account that stores the value of all consumed raw materials while the Production Order is in process. WIP value will pass from one WIP account to the next WIP account when the Production Order progresses through the phases of the production process (e.g. Wort WIP -> Green Beer WIP -> Bright Beer WIP).

Upon completion of the Production Order, the total value from all consumed raw materials is passed to the account assigned to the Output Product on the Production Order. This functionality has not changed with the addition of Production Stage Groups.

Fields And Definitions

  1. Define the phases of the production process that you wish to capture WIP value while production is in process.
    a. As previously stated, the best practice for brewing production phases is Wort WIP -> Green Beer WIP -> Bright Beer WIP. However, a single In-Process WIP phase is also acceptable.
    ​
    b. This does not apply to the packaging phase, only the phases leading up to packaging.
    ​
    ​

  2. Create one WIP Product Type for each production phase.
    ​
    Product Type Fields:
    a.Track Inventory = True
    ​
    b.Type Code = WIP
    ​
    c. Store in Equipment = True
    ​
    ​

  3. Product Type Account Mapping
    ​
    a. Link all WIP Product Types to an Inventory Asset Account Maps record that links to the Inventory Asset Account that will store the value of this phase.
    ​
    ​

  4. Create one Production Stage Group for each production phase.
    ​
    Production Stage Group Fields:
    a. Product Type = set the WIP Product Type created in step 2.
    ​
    b. Package = set the unit of measure Package that you would want set by default on the auto-created WIP Products.
    -BBLs is commonly used on beer Production Stage Groups.
    ​
    -Gallons is commonly used on spirit Production Stage Groups.
    ​
    ​

  5. Link all non-packaging Production Stage Types to the Production Stage Group that best represents the stage’s production phase.
    ​
    For example, Production Stage Types: Mash, Lauter, Boil, & Whirlpool are commonly grouped under the ‘Wort’ phase, and therefore would be placed under a ‘Wort WIP’ Production Stage Group.
    a. Once this setup is in place, WIP Products will auto-generate for each Production Stage Group + Recipe Brand.
    ​
    b. These WIP Products map to a WIP Account where the value of the WIP is stored while the Production Order is in process.
    ​
    c. These WIP Products are automatically set on each Recipe Stage.

Best Practices

All of the examples provided in this Help Resource have been focused on the general best practice of using Production Stage Groups, WIP Products, and WIP Accounts to represent the three common phases of the brewing process: Wort WIP -> Green Beer WIP -> Bright Beer WIP. This is the general best practice because these phases best represent the major physical transformation processes and change to accumulate WIP value as a result of this transformation. While this is the general best practice, this is not the only way that Production Stage Groups, WIP Products, and WIP Accounts can be used.
​
​

The Production Stage Group solution supports a setup as simple as a single generic ‘In-Process WIP’ Production Stage Group, where all Production Stage Types share the same ‘In-Process WIP’ Production Stage Group. This simple setup stores the value of all consumed raw materials in a single WIP Account while Production Orders are in process, and then passes the final value of all consumed raw materials to the account mapped to the Output Product when the Production Order is completed.

16990066:
Distributor troubleshooting for dropped 820 EDI remittances (Dropped payment amount errors) in Encompass: missing PO numbers, pre-paid invoices, and missing AR accounts on the exchange configuration. v25.01+.

Minimum Version Required: 25.01

Pre-Conditions

The 820 remittance is a standardized electronic format used to send payment-related information between trading partners. It typically includes details such as:
​
​

  • Payment amount
    ​
    ​

  • Invoice numbers being paid
    ​
    ​

  • Adjustments or deductions
    ​
    ​

  • Payment date
    ​
    ​

  • Other relevant payment information

Steps

Troubleshooting Steps:
​
​

  1. Verify PO Numbers: Ensure that all invoices have accurate and complete PO numbers. Work with your distribution and sales teams to improve PO entry practices. This is the most critical step
    ​
    ​

  2. Check for Pre-Payments: Before processing remittances, verify if any invoices have been manually paid. If an invoice has been paid and its balance is zero, the corresponding remittance may be dropped. Reconcile these situations manually. Investigate why manual payments are occurring before remittances are processed and implement process improvements to prevent this.
    ​
    ​

  3. Review Exchange Configuration AR Accounts:

    • Navigate to the relevant Exchange Configuration.
      ​
      ​

    • Verify that all relevant AR Accounts are listed in the "Exchange Configurations AR Accounts" section. If this section is empty or missing the necessary accounts, add them. This ensures that if the system can identify the AR account but cannot apply the payment, it can still create a payment invoice.
      ​
      ​

    • Consider consolidating AR accounts if they all flow through the same entity. This can simplify the configuration and reduce potential errors.
      ​
      ​

  4. Investigate Specific Examples: When encountering a dropped remittance, examine the associated Exchange Task ID and Loadsheet ID. Review the corresponding invoice to identify any missing or incorrect PO numbers. Check the invoice balance to see if it was previously paid.
    ​
    ​

  5. Analyze Payment Discrepancies: Compare bank deposits with processed remittances. Identify any discrepancies and investigate the corresponding Exchange Task IDs to determine the cause of the dropped payments.

Fields And Definitions

  • EDIStatus: A field which will show the last type of EDI sent on the invoice. This can be used to resend EDI by manually changing the EDI Status
    ​
    ​

  • Remittance: A document containing payments that have occurred

Best Practices

Troubleshooting Dropped Remittances (820 Errors)

This document outlines the troubleshooting steps for resolving issues with dropped remittances, indicated by "Dropped payment amount of X" errors in the 820 remittance information. This issue can lead to discrepancies between remittances and bank deposits.
​
​

Problem:

820 remittances are being dropped by the system, resulting in unapplied payments and potential reconciliation issues. This often occurs when the system cannot locate a corresponding invoice using the provided PO number. While the system typically leaves unapplied amounts on the loadsheet when a PO is missing, in these cases, the entire remittance amount is dropped.
​
​

Root Causes:

  1. Missing or Incorrect PO Numbers: The 820 remittance uses the PO number to match payments to invoices. If the invoice lacks a PO number, or the PO number is incorrect, the system cannot automatically apply the payment. This is the most common cause.
    ​
    ​

  2. Zeroed-Out Invoices: If an invoice has already been paid (manually or otherwise) before the remittance arrives, the system may drop the remittance. The EDI logic is designed to drop remittances for invoices with a zero balance.
    ​
    ​

  3. Missing AR Account in Exchange Configuration: If the system can identify the AR account but cannot apply the payment (due to a missing or incorrect PO, for example), it attempts to create a payment invoice on the AR account specified in the exchange configuration. If no AR account is defined in the exchange configuration, the payment is dropped.
    ​
    ​

Recommendations:

  • Process Improvement: Review internal payment processes to avoid manual payments of invoices that will have remittances coming through.
    ​
    ​

  • Regular Reconciliation: Regularly reconcile bank deposits with processed remittances to identify and address any discrepancies promptly.
    ​
    ​

  • System Settings Review: Check system setting "Automatically set EDI Remittance Load Sheets to this Status" (e.g., setting 342) to ensure it's configured appropriately.
    ​
    ​

  • Collaboration with Encompass Support: If the issue persists, contact Encompass support and provide them with specific examples (Exchange Task IDs, Loadsheet IDs, Invoice numbers) for further investigation.

How to Use Fusion Report View

Generate Purchase Orders:

    ​

How the Automated Transfer is created:
​
​1. Once the shipment is received in the "primary" location, the AutoTransfers_From_TransferToPurchaseTransactions scheduled task will run within 15 minutes and a transfer invoice will be created for the "primary" location
​

4. The transfer purchase for the "other" locations will be created using the existing transfer planner EDI logic.
​
5. Once the transfer invoice is created, the transfer to location will be cleared out on the original purchase. This is to prevent duplicate transfers from being created.

  • Click the Sub Table button and select Alert Users
